    11. Hibernate

    The previous chapter showed how a Java application communicates with a database through a driver JDBC: a connection is opened, commands SQL are written, the rows of the result are read column by column, and they are copied into objects. This process of copying—from rows to objects and from objects to the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands—is repetitive. It can be automated using a tool: an “Object-Relational Mapper” (ORM). This chapter introduces the most widely used ORM in the Java world, Hibernate, and the standard it implements, Jakarta Persistence.

    The chapter revisits the sample database from the articles in Chapter 10 and concludes with version 7 of the tax calculation application, whose ORM layer uses Hibernate.

    11.1. What is a ORM?

    11.1.1. Objects and Tables

    A Java application works with objects: an item has a name, a price, and a stock level; an order has a customer and a list of line items, each of which refers to an item. A relational database stores this same information in tables: one row in the [articles] table per item, one row in the [commandes] table per order, with the relationships between rows expressed by foreign keys. The two worlds do not quite align:

    • an object directly references other objects ([commande.getClient()]); a row contains the primary key value of another row ([client_id]);
    • an object can contain a collection ([commande.getLignes()]); a table contains only single values; the collection is represented by the rows of another table that point to the order;
    • Java types ([String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate], [boolean]) and the types SQL ([varchar(30)], [decimal(10,2)], [date], [bit]) are not the same;
    • objects are queried using Java (and the API stream), while tables are queried using SQL.

    A ORM bridges the two worlds. We define the correspondence between classes and tables (the model, or “mapping”) once and for all; it then takes care of:

    • translating queries written in a language that refers to objects (HQL) or constructed by Java code (the API Criteria);
    • to create objects from the read lines (this is called materialization);
    • to store the read objects and detect those that have been modified, added, or deleted;
    • generate the [INSERT], [UPDATE], and [DELETE] commands that reflect these changes in the database;
    • and, if necessary, to create and update the database schema (tables, columns, indexes) based on the classes.

    The architecture of an application that uses Hibernate with MySQL is as follows:

    • [1]: the application. Its [dao] layer no longer communicates directly with the JDBC driver but with Hibernate, through a [Session] object and HQL queries;
    • [2]: Hibernate, independent of SGBD: model, query translation, change tracking, schema generation;
    • [3]: the dialect specific to SGBD (here, [MySQLDialect]): it knows the SQL syntax of SGBD, its column types, and its functions. The dialects of the main SGBDs are part of Hibernate itself: nothing needs to be added to the project;
    • [4]: the JDBC driver for SGBD, the one from Chapter 10 (MySQL Connector/J): Hibernate does not replace JDBC; it uses it;
    • [5]: the SGBD.

    11.1.2. Jakarta Persistence and Hibernate

    Hibernate was created in 2001 by Gavin King in response to the cumbersomeness of the “entity beans” in the Java EE platform of the time. Its success was such that its concepts were incorporated into a standard, JPA (Java Persistence API), released in 2006 with Java EE 5. When Java EE was transferred to the Eclipse Foundation and renamed Jakarta EE, JPA became Jakarta Persistence, and its packages changed from [javax.persistence] to [jakarta.persistence] (version 3.0, 2020). The current version is Jakarta Persistence 3.2 (2024).

    Jakarta Persistence is a specification: a set of interfaces ([EntityManagerFactory], [EntityManager]...), annotations ([@Entity], [@Id], [@Column]...), and a query language, JPQL. It is implemented by several products: Hibernate ORM (the most widely used, used by Spring Boot and Quarkus), EclipseLink (the reference implementation)... This course uses Hibernate ORM 7.4.5, which implements Jakarta Persistence 3.2.

    Hibernate offers two ways to use it:

    • exclusively through the standard interfaces: in this case, the code depends only on [jakarta.persistence], and it would in principle be possible to switch implementations;
    • through its own, more feature-rich “native” API, whose interfaces extend those of the standard: a [SessionFactory] is a [EntityManagerFactory], and a [Session] is a [EntityManager].

    We use Hibernate’s own API, as recommended in its documentation: It provides all the standard methods ([persist], [find], [merge], [remove]...) as well as Hibernate’s extensions. The annotations, on the other hand, are always those defined by the standard. The following table shows the correspondences:

    Jakarta Persistence
    Hibernate
    Role
    [EntityManagerFactory]
    [SessionFactory]
    Hibernate configuration for a database: a heavy object, created once, shared by the entire application
    [EntityManager]
    [Session]
    A database session: a lightweight, short-lived object
    [EntityTransaction]
    [Transaction]
    a transaction
    JPQL
    HQL
    the query language; HQL is a superset of JPQL
    [CriteriaBuilder]
    [HibernateCriteriaBuilder]
    Query construction using Java code

    11.1.3. Libraries

    The libraries used in this chapter are as follows (they are summarized in the appendix on Maven dependencies):

    Maven Dependency
    Role
    [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-core] 7.4.5.Final
    Hibernate itself; it includes the API from Jakarta Persistence 3.2 ([jakarta.persistence-api]) and its own dependencies (Byte Buddy for class generation, ANTLR for query analysis, JBoss Logging for logging, etc.)
    [com.mysql:mysql-connector-j] 9.7.0
    the JDBC driver for MySQL, the one from Chapter 10
    [ch.qos.logback:logback-classic] 1.5.38
    Logback, which will receive the Hibernate log

    Hibernate writes its log (executed SQL commands, warnings, etc.) through JBoss Logging, a small library that simply forwards messages to the logging system it finds in the classpath: Log4j 2, or Logback (via SLF4J), or, failing that, the one from JDK or [java.util.logging]. Without configuration, the latter displays each message on two lines, in red in most consoles, which makes the program output difficult to read. We therefore add Logback to our projects and configure it using a [logback.xml] file.

    11.1.4. Code First or Database First

    The model (the mapping between classes and tables) can be built in two ways:

    • "code first": we write the Java classes, and Hibernate derives the database schema from them, which it can create on its own. This is the approach taken in this chapter;
    • "Database First": The database already exists, and classes are generated from its schema using Hibernate’s reverse-engineering tools (Hibernate Tools) or those of the development environments (IntelliJ IDEA can generate entities from database tables). This is the approach for applications that need to work with an existing database. The generated code is similar to what we would write by hand.

    package premier;

import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// A store item: a regular Java class, plus a few annotations
@Entity
public class Article {

     // The primary key, generated by SGBD
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;
     // the other columns in the table
    private String nom;
    private BigDecimal prix;
    private int stockActuel;
    private int stockMinimum;

     // the parameterless constructor required by Hibernate
    protected Article() {
    }

     // the constructor used by the program
    public Article(String nom, BigDecimal prix, int stockActuel, int stockMinimum) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.prix = prix;
        this.stockActuel = stockActuel;
        this.stockMinimum = stockMinimum;
    }

     // display
    @Override
    public String toString() {
        return "[%d, %s, %.2f, %d, %d]".formatted(id, nom, prix, stockActuel, stockMinimum);
    }
}
    • Line 10: The annotation [@Entity] (package [jakarta.persistence]) makes the class an entity. It is almost a regular Java class, deriving from no Hibernate class: it is referred to as POJO (“Plain Old Java Object”);
    • lines 14–16: the primary key is designated by the [@Id] annotation. There is no naming convention: the annotation is required. [@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)] indicates that its values will be generated by SGBD (the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column of MySQL). Its type is [Integer], not [int]: the value [null] means “not yet recorded in the database”;
    • lines 18–21: Each field in the class becomes a column with the same name. Since the annotation [@Id] is applied to a field, Hibernate accesses the fields directly (it reads and writes them via reflection, even if they are private): the class does not need accessors;
    • lines 24–25: Jakarta Persistence requires a parameterless constructor, which Hibernate uses to create objects read from the database. It can be protected ([protected]): the application code will not use it;
    • lines 28–33: the constructor used by the program. No identifier is provided; it will be generated by SGBD;
    • lines 36–39: a convenient display of the item. The [%.2f] format displays the price with two decimal places, in accordance with local conventions (a comma in France).

    An entity cannot be a record (Chapter 4): Hibernate must be able to create the empty object, fill in its fields, and modify those fields when the application changes them—something that the immutability of a record prevents. Records remain very useful with Hibernate for query results that are not entities (projections), as we will see.

    11.2.3. [SessionFactory] and [Session]

    The program uses three Hibernate objects:

    • [SessionFactory] represents Hibernate configured for a database: the list of entities, the database, and the options. Its creation is resource-intensive (Hibernate analyzes the entities, connects to the server to determine its version, and prepares the SQL for common operations): only one is created per database and per application, at startup. It is thread-safe: all threads in the application can use it;
    • The [Session] represents a work session with the database. It establishes a connection when needed, stores the records it has read or saved, and is able to update the database with any changes. It is a lightweight, short-lived object that is not thread-safe: one is opened for each unit of work and then closed;
    • [Transaction]: With Hibernate, all writes to the database occur within an explicit transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] (commit) or [rollback] (rollback).

    [SessionFactory] and [Session] implement the [AutoCloseable] interface: they are created in a [try] statement with resources, which closes them at the end of the block.

    package premier;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // the SessionFactory: Hibernate configured for the [hbpremier] database
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("premier")
                 // the entities
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                 // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbpremier?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                 // display of SQL orders, formatted, without colors
                .showSql(true, true, false)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

             // the tables are deleted and then recreated from the entities
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);

             // Adds three items in a single transaction
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                IO.println("--- persist");
                session.persist(new Article("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), 10, 5));
                session.persist(new Article("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(10), 10, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("arc", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), 4, 1));
                IO.println("--- commit");
                transaction.commit();
            }

             // Reading the table with a new session
            IO.println("--- lecture des articles");
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by nom", Article.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    IO.println(article);
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
    • lines 14–22: creation of [SessionFactory]. There are several ways to configure Hibernate (we’ll discuss them later); we use the [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration] class from Hibernate 7, an enhanced version of the [PersistenceConfiguration] class introduced with Jakarta Persistence 3.2, which allows everything to be configured via code. Its parameter is the name of the persistence unit—a freely chosen name that appears in Hibernate messages. Each method returns the configuration itself, allowing calls to be chained together;
    • line 16: the list of entities;
    • lines 18–19: the URL and JDBC from the [hbpremier] database, in the same format as in Chapter 10, and the user ([root], with no password in Laragon). The [createDatabaseIfNotExist=true] parameter of URL is an option of the MySQL driver: it creates the database if it does not exist;
    • Line 21: [showSql(true, true, false)] instructs Hibernate to print each SQL command it executes to the console, formatted across multiple lines (second parameter), without colors (third parameter). Looking at the SQL sent to the server is the best way to understand what Hibernate is doing: we’ll do this in all the examples;
    • line 22: [createEntityManagerFactory] constructs [SessionFactory] (the method name follows the standard; the returned type is Hibernate’s);
    • Lines 25–26: The [SchemaManager] object from [SessionFactory] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) manages the entity tables: [drop(false)] deletes them if they exist, [create(false)] creates them (the [false] parameter specifies that the database itself should not be deleted or created). This is convenient for examples and tests; a real-world application manages its database differently, as we will see;
    • line 29: [openSession()] opens a session;
    • line 30: the start of a transaction;
    • lines 32–34: [persist] adds three new items to the session: they will be saved to the database. No value is specified for the identifier; it will be generated by SGBD;
    • line 36: [commit] commits the transaction. Prior to this, the session sends the SQL commands to the server, which are still necessary to save the changes it has stored: this is referred to as “flushing” the session to the database;
    • lines 42–44: a query written in HQL, Hibernate’s query language: the items in alphabetical order by name. It refers to the entity [Article] and its field [nom], not to the table. The second parameter of [createSelectionQuery] is the result type: [getResultList] returns a [List<Article>].

    Comments:

    • Lines 2–17: Hibernate informational messages: the name of the persistence unit, the Hibernate version, and database characteristics (URL, driver, selected dialect, server version, transaction isolation level, connection pool size). Hibernate queried the server to select the [MySQLDialect] dialect appropriate for its version;
    • line 4: a warning. Hibernate manages its own small connection pool, which is not intended for a production application. We’ll see, with Spring, how to provide it with the HikariCP pool from Chapter 10; for our examples, the built-in pool is sufficient;
    • Lines 18–28: Deletion and subsequent creation of table [Article] based on the entity: the table name is the same as the entity name, the columns have the same names as the fields, and the column [id] is the primary key with a generated value ([auto_increment]). The columns for primitive-type fields ([int]) are [not null]: a [int] cannot equal [null]. Those for reference-type fields ([String], [BigDecimal]) accept the value [NULL];
    • note the default types: [varchar(255)] for a string, and [decimal(38,2)] for a [BigDecimal] (38 digits, including 2 decimal places). These are rarely the ones you want: the following paragraph shows how to specify them;
    • Lines 29–51: The three configured [INSERT] commands were executed as soon as [persist] was called, before [commit]. This is a consequence of the key being generated by SGBD ([IDENTITY]): the session must know an entity’s identifier as soon as it takes over that entity, and to obtain it, it must execute the insert operation (the JDBC driver returns the generated key; see Chapter 10). With other generation methods, the insert operations are deferred until the session is synchronized. The parameter values ([?]) are not displayed: we will see how to make them appear;
    • lines 53–63: the query HQL [from Article order by nom] was translated into a [SELECT ... ORDER BY] statement. Hibernate assigned the alias [a1_0] to the table and created a [Article] object for each row read (lines 64–66).

    We did not write any SQL statements or any column-reading code: that is the whole point of a ORM. We can also see that this does not eliminate the need to understand SQL: to determine whether the generated SQL is correct and effective, you need to know how to read it.

    11.3. The Model

    Hibernate builds its model from entities in three steps:

    • First, it applies its default rules: anything that isn’t specified is assigned a reasonable value (this is known as “configuration by exception”);
    • it then supplements or corrects these values using the annotations placed on the entities;
    • finally, it applies the mapping files XML ([orm.xml]), which can fully describe a class without annotations or modify what its annotations specify.

    11.3.1. Default Rules

    We saw the basics of this in the first example:

    • an entity carries the annotation [@Entity] and has an identifier designated by [@Id]; both of these annotations are required;
    • the placement of the annotation [@Id] determines the access mode: when placed on a field, Hibernate reads and writes the fields directly; When placed on an accessor ([getId]), access occurs through the accessors ([getX]/[setX]). Access via fields is the most common: it allows the class to have whatever methods it wants;
    • any non-static field is stored in a column, unless it bears the annotation [@Transient] or the keyword [transient];
    • the table name is the entity name (the class’s simple name), and the column name is the field name. These names are then processed by a naming strategy: Hibernate’s strategy keeps the names as-is, while another strategy—which we’ll try below—converts them to “snake case” ([stockActuel] becomes [stock_actuel]). Spring Boot uses the latter by default;
    • A column of a primitive type ([int], [double], [boolean]) is [NOT NULL]; a column of a reference type ([Integer], [String], [BigDecimal], [LocalDate]) accepts the value [NULL];
    • the types SQL are selected by the dialect. With MySQL: [integer] for [int], [bigint] for [long], [bit] for [boolean], [varchar(255)] for [String], [decimal(38,2)] for [BigDecimal], [date] for [LocalDate], [datetime(6)] (to the microsecond) for [LocalDateTime]. By default, an enumeration is recorded by its sequence number (see Chapter 3); the annotation [@Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)] records it by its name, which is more reliable;
    • a field that refers to another entity, or to a collection of entities, defines a relationship (we’ll discuss this later).

    package modele;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.Transient;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;

// an entity configured by annotations
@Entity
@Table(name = "produits")
public class Produit {

     // the primary key: @Id, regardless of its name
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer code;

     // required string of up to 50 characters
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    private String nom;

     // optional string (column NULL) of up to 200 characters
    @Column(length = 200)
    private String description;

     // Column name and type (SQL) are required
    @Column(name = "prix_ht", nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal prixHT;

     // an optional date: an object may be null
    private LocalDate dateRetrait;

     // a field without a column
    @Transient
    private boolean selectionne;

    protected Produit() {
    }

     // A method is never registered: Hibernate accesses fields here, not methods
    public BigDecimal getPrixTTC() {
        return prixHT.multiply(new BigDecimal("1.2"));
    }

    public boolean isSelectionne() {
        return selectionne;
    }
}
    • lines 3–9: Jakarta Persistence annotations;
    • line 15: [@Table] specifies the table name;
    • lines 19–21: the primary key, designated by [@Id] regardless of its name;
    • lines 24–25: [@Column] specifies the column; [nullable = false] makes it required ([NOT NULL]), [length = 50] sets its length ([varchar(50)]);
    • lines 28–29: an optional description of up to 200 characters; the column will accept the value [NULL];
    • lines 32–33: [@Column] also specifies the column name ([prix_ht]) and, for a decimal number, its precision (the total number of digits) and its scale (the number of digits after the decimal point): [decimal(10,2)];
    • line 36: an optional date. The type [LocalDate] (Chapter 5) represents a date without a time: it is associated with the types SQL and [date];
    • lines 39–40: [@Transient] excludes a field from the model: in this case, information useful to the user interface that does not belong in the database;
    • lines 46–48: a method, even if named like a getter, is not registered, since Hibernate accesses the fields directly. If accessed via getters, the annotation [@Transient] would need to be added to it.

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- the mapping of the class [Fournisseur] to its table, described in XML (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) -->
<entity-mappings xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm"
                 xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance"
                 xsi:schemaLocation="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm
                                     https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/persistence/orm/orm_3_2.xsd"
                 version="3.2">
    <entity class="modele.Fournisseur" access="FIELD">
        <table name="fournisseurs">
             <!-- a unique index: two suppliers cannot have the same company name -->
            <index name="ix_fournisseurs_raison_sociale" column-list="raisonSociale" unique="true"/>
        </table>
        <attributes>
            <id name="numero">
                <generated-value strategy="IDENTITY"/>
            </id>
            <basic name="raisonSociale">
                <column nullable="false" length="60"/>
            </basic>
            <basic name="telephone">
                <column name="tel" length="20"/>
            </basic>
             <!-- a default value calculated by SGBD: Hibernate never writes to this column -->
            <basic name="dateCreation">
                <column nullable="false" insertable="false" updatable="false"
                        column-definition="datetime(6) default current_timestamp(6)"/>
            </basic>
        </attributes>
    </entity>
</entity-mappings>
    • lines 3–7: the XML schema for Jakarta Persistence 3.2 mapping files;
    • line 8: the described class, with access via fields;
    • lines 9–12: the table, and a unique index on the company name: no two suppliers can have the same one. The equivalent annotation is [@Table(name = "fournisseurs", indexes = @Index(...))];
    • lines 14–16: the identifier, generated by SGBD;
    • lines 17–19: a required column of no more than 60 characters;
    • Lines 20–22: The field [telephone] is stored in the column [tel];
    • lines 24–27: The creation date has a default value, calculated by SGBD. The [column-definition] attribute returns the text SQL from the column definition, copied verbatim in the order [CREATE TABLE]; [insertable="false"] and [updatable="false"] indicate that Hibernate must never write to this column, which allows SGBD to use [current_timestamp(6)].

    Everything that annotations do can be done in XML. Annotations have the advantage of placing the configuration next to the field, and this is the most common approach; the XML file, on the other hand, keeps the classes independent of Jakarta Persistence and consolidates the configuration in a single location. The two approaches can be combined: the XML file takes precedence in case of a conflict. Jakarta Persistence does not support configuring the model via Java code, as other frameworks (such as Entity Framework in C#) do.

    package modele;

import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.Attribute;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.EntityType;
import jakarta.persistence.metamodel.SingularAttribute;
import java.io.StringWriter;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // The table creation script will be written to this object
        StringWriter script = new StringWriter();
         // a SessionFactory that never connects to the server
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("modele")
                 // An annotated entity and a mapping described in XML
                .managedClass(Produit.class)
                .mappingFile("META-INF/fournisseur.orm.xml")
                 // no database: SGBD and its version are provided for the SQL dialect
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_NAME, "MySQL")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_DB_MAJOR_VERSION, "8")
                .property(AvailableSettings.ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT, false)
                 // column names in "snake case": raisonSociale -> raison_sociale
                .property(AvailableSettings.PHYSICAL_NAMING_STRATEGY,
                        PhysicalNamingStrategySnakeCaseImpl.class.getName())
                 // the table creation script, without executing it
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, "create")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
                .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {

             // the model built by Hibernate: entities and attributes (API Jakarta Persistence)
            for (EntityType<?> entite : sessionFactory.getMetamodel().getEntities()) {
                IO.println("entité %s (%s)".formatted(entite.getName(), entite.getJavaType().getName()));
                for (Attribute<?, ?> attribut : entite.getAttributes()) {
                    boolean id = attribut instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId();
                    IO.println("  %-14s %s%s".formatted(attribut.getName(),
                            attribut.getJavaType().getSimpleName(), id ? " (identifiant)" : ""));
                }
            }
        }
         // the table creation script, without removing 4 spaces from its lines
        IO.println("--- script de création");
        script.toString().strip().lines()
                .map(ligne -> ligne.startsWith("    ") ? ligne.substring(4) : ligne)
                .forEach(ligne -> IO.println(ligne.stripTrailing()));
    }
}
    • line 16: a [StringWriter] (package [java.io]), a write stream to a string in memory, will receive the SQL script;
    • lines 20–21: the annotated entity is declared by [managedClass], and the file XML by [mappingFile];
    • lines 23–25: The database [hbmodele] will never exist; this [SessionFactory] is used solely to examine the model. Therefore, there is no URL or JDBC. To select the SQL dialect without querying the server, Hibernate needs the name of the SGBD and its version; the property [ALLOW_METADATA_ON_BOOT] ([hibernate.boot.allow_jdbc_metadata_access]) prevents it from connecting at startup. The names of the configuration properties are constants in the [AvailableSettings] interface;
    • lines 27–28: the “snake case” naming convention;
    • lines 30–33: Hibernate will write the table creation script (["create"]) to the [script] object without executing it; the commands are terminated by a semicolon and formatted across multiple lines;
    • line 37: the [getMetamodel] method (Jakarta Persistence) provides access to the model: its entities ([EntityType]) and, for each, its attributes ([Attribute]);
    • lines 38–43: for each entity, its name and class; for each attribute, its name, its Java type, and whether it is the identifier. The pattern filtering in line 40 ([instanceof SingularAttribute<?, ?> s && s.isId()], Chapter 4) checks the attribute’s type and, if appropriate, uses it immediately;
    • lines 48–50: the script output, without the four spaces that Hibernate adds to its lines.

    11.3.3. Generated identifiers

    The annotation [@GeneratedValue] indicates that the identifier value is generated. Its parameter [strategy] specifies how:

    Strategy
    Generating the ID
    [IDENTITY]
    by SGBD, when inserting the row (column [AUTO_INCREMENT] from MySQL, [IDENTITY] from SQL Server, and PostgreSQL)
    [SEQUENCE]
    by a sequence from SGBD (PostgreSQL, Oracle), which Hibernate queries before insertion
    [TABLE]
    by a counter table managed by Hibernate
    [UUID]
    by Hibernate: a random universal identifier, such as [java.util.UUID]
    [AUTO] (by default)
    Hibernate chooses; with MySQL, which has no sequences, it simulates them using a table named [<table>_SEQ]

    With MySQL, we still use [IDENTITY], which corresponds to the natural behavior of the [AUTO_INCREMENT] column. We’ve seen the result of this: the [INSERT] command is executed as soon as [persist] is called, and Hibernate cannot group multiple inserts into a batch (we’ll cover batches later). The [SEQUENCE] strategy, which allows you to know the ID before the insertion, is preferred for SGBD statements that use sequences.

    11.3.4. Optional Values and [NULL] Columns

    Whether a column is optional is therefore determined in Java by the field type (primitive or reference) and by the [nullable] attribute of [@Column]. This choice must be made carefully: the rule expresses both a constraint in the Java code (“this value may be missing”) and a constraint in the database. A few notes:

    • [@Column(nullable = false)] defines the [NOT NULL] constraint in the schema created by Hibernate, and Hibernate also uses it before sending a [INSERT] or [UPDATE] command: if the field is [null], it does not send the command and throws a [PropertyValueException] error (“not-null property references a null or transient value”). This Hibernate check is disabled by default when Jakarta Validation (below) is present: validation then falls back to its annotations, or, failing that, to SGBD, which rejects the command;
    • For a more comprehensive validation performed by Java before any database access, Jakarta Validation (library [hibernate-validator]) and its annotations [@NotNull], [@Size(max = 30)], [@Positive] are used.. When present in the classpath, Hibernate validates entities before saving them and takes these annotations into account when creating columns;
    • a field cannot be of type [Optional] (Chapter 4), which is not intended for this purpose; however, an accessor can return a [Optional] constructed from an optional field: [return Optional.ofNullable(description);].

    11.4. The following examples: two common libraries

    The examples in the following paragraphs almost all use the [hbarticles] database and its [articles] table, populated with the six items from Chapter 10. Rather than repeating the Hibernate entity and configuration in each module, we place them in a library—the [articles] module—on which the other modules depend. We also replace the SQL log from [showSql]—which is too verbose for our examples—with a more compact log, placed in a second library, the [outils] module.

    11.4.1. The compact SQL log

    Rather than writing directly to the console ([showSql]), Hibernate can forward its activity to the logging system (in this case, Logback), with each message category written to a different logger:

    Log
    Level
    Messages
    [org.hibernate.SQL]
    [DEBUG]
    SQL orders executed
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind]
    [TRACE]
    the value of each parameter in an order SQL
    [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc]
    [TRACE]
    including, among other things, the initiation, confirmation, and cancellation of transactions
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch]
    [TRACE]
    execution of order batches SQL
    [org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error]
    [WARN]
    Errors reported by SGBD

    A log only records messages of a level equal to or higher than its own. Therefore, you simply need to set the desired level for these logs in the [logback.xml] file to retrieve these messages. We pass them through a layout class that makes them more compact:

    package outils;

import ch.qos.logback.classic.Level;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.spi.ILoggingEvent;
import ch.qos.logback.core.LayoutBase;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

// A compact log of SQL commands executed by Hibernate: a Logback layout
public class JournalSql extends LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent> {

     // the Hibernate loggers used
    public static final String SQL = "org.hibernate.SQL";
    public static final String PARAMETRES = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind";
    public static final String TRANSACTIONS = "org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc";
    public static final String ERREURS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error";
    public static final String LOTS = "org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch";

     // the maximum length of a clause written on a single line
    private static final int LARGEUR = 100;

     // Execution of a batch of SQL commands: “Executing JDBC batch (3 / 3) - [...]”
    private static final Pattern LOT = Pattern.compile("Executing JDBC batch \\((\\d+) / \\d+\\).*");

     // a parameter associated with an order SQL: “binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [vélo]”
    private static final Pattern PARAMETRE =
            Pattern.compile("binding parameter \\((\\d+):\\w+\\) <- \\[(.*)]");

     // message layout: the text to be written is rendered ("": nothing is written)
    @Override
    public String doLayout(ILoggingEvent evenement) {
        String message = evenement.getFormattedMessage();
        return switch (evenement.getLoggerName()) {
            case SQL -> ordreSql(message);
            case PARAMETRES -> parametre(message);
            case TRANSACTIONS -> transaction(message);
            case ERREURS -> erreur(message);
            case LOTS -> lot(message);
            default -> "";
        };
    }

     // the SQL query formatted by Hibernate, made more compact: one line per clause (select, from...)
    private static String ordreSql(String sql) {
         // non-empty lines, without trailing spaces
        List<String> lignes = sql.lines().map(String::stripTrailing).filter(l -> !l.isBlank()).toList();
         // the clauses: a top-level line (least indented) and the lines that follow it
        int retrait = lignes.stream().mapToInt(JournalSql::retrait).min().orElse(0);
        List<List<String>> clauses = new ArrayList<>();
        for (String ligne : lignes) {
            if (clauses.isEmpty() || retrait(ligne) == retrait) {
                clauses.add(new ArrayList<>());
            }
            clauses.getLast().add(ligne.substring(retrait));
        }
         // each clause is written on a single line, if it is not too long
        StringBuilder texte = new StringBuilder();
        String debut = "";
        for (List<String> clause : clauses) {
            String ligne = debut + clause.stream().map(String::strip).collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
            if (ligne.equals("insert") || ligne.equals("delete")) {
                 // [insert into ...], [delete from ...]: a single line
                debut = ligne + " ";
                continue;
            }
            if (ligne.length() <= LARGEUR) {
                texte.append("    SQL> ").append(ligne).append('\n');
            } else {
                 // Clause too long: we keep the lines from Hibernate
                for (int i = 0; i < clause.size(); i++) {
                    texte.append("    SQL> ").append(i == 0 ? debut : "").append(clause.get(i)).append('\n');
                }
            }
            debut = "";
        }
        return texte.toString();
    }

     // the number of spaces at the beginning of the line
    private static int retrait(String ligne) {
        return ligne.length() - ligne.stripLeading().length();
    }

     // the value of a parameter in the order SQL
    private static String parametre(String message) {
        Matcher m = PARAMETRE.matcher(message);
        return m.matches() ? "    SQL> -- paramètre " + m.group(1) + " = " + m.group(2) + "\n" : "";
    }

     // start, commit, and rollback of transactions (other messages are ignored)
    private static String transaction(String message) {
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003002")) {
            return "    SQL> -- début de transaction\n";
        }
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003004")) {
            return "    SQL> -- transaction validée (COMMIT)\n";
        }
        if (message.startsWith("HHH10003006")) {
            return "    SQL> -- transaction annulée (ROLLBACK)\n";
        }
        return "";
    }

     // the error reported by SGBD (the line containing its error codes is ignored)
    private static String erreur(String message) {
        return message.startsWith("HHH000247") ? "" : "    SQL> -- échec : " + message + "\n";
    }

     // Execution of a batch of orders SQL (other messages are ignored)
    private static String lot(String message) {
        Matcher m = LOT.matcher(message);
        return m.matches() ? "    SQL> -- exécution d'un lot de " + m.group(1) + " ordre(s)\n" : "";
    }

     // Executes an action without logging SQL
    public static void sansJournal(Runnable action) {
        List<Logger> journaux = Stream.of(SQL, PARAMETRES, TRANSACTIONS, ERREURS, LOTS)
                .map(JournalSql::journal)
                .toList();
         // the current levels, restored at the end
        List<Level> niveaux = journaux.stream().map(Logger::getLevel).toList();
        journaux.forEach(j -> j.setLevel(Level.OFF));
        try {
            action.run();
        } finally {
            for (int i = 0; i < journaux.size(); i++) {
                journaux.get(i).setLevel(niveaux.get(i));
            }
        }
    }

     // the Logback log with the specified name
    private static Logger journal(String nom) {
        return (Logger) LoggerFactory.getLogger(nom);
    }
}
    • line 16: a Logback layout class derives from the [LayoutBase<ILoggingEvent>] class; its [doLayout] method (lines 36–47) receives each message (a [ILoggingEvent]) and returns the text to be written;
    • lines 19–23: the names of the Hibernate logs used;
    • lines 39–46: the processing depends on the log that sent the message ([switch] on a string, using the Java 14 “arrow” syntax);
    • lines 50–83: the order SQL, as formatted by Hibernate ([format_sql]), spread across multiple lines, with one column per line. We make it more compact. Non-empty lines are organized into clauses (lines 54–61): a clause begins with a top-level line ([select], [from], [where]...) and includes the indented lines that follow it. Each clause is then written on a single line, preceded by [SQL>], if it does not exceed 100 characters (lines 72–73); otherwise, its lines are retained (lines 76–78). The clauses [insert] and [delete] are combined with the next one (lines 67–71);
    • lines 91–94: The Hibernate message that provides a parameter’s value looks like [binding parameter (1:VARCHAR) <- [vélo]]. The regular expression in lines 32–33 (Chapter 5) extracts the parameter number and its value;
    • lines 97–108: Among the many messages in the [org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc] log, only those indicating the start, commit, and rollback of a transaction are retained. Each Hibernate message begins with a code ([HHH10003002]...) that uniquely identifies it;
    • lines 111–113: an error in SGBD. Hibernate writes this as two messages: one containing the error codes (which we ignore) and the other containing the error text;
    • lines 116–119: execution of a batch of SQL commands, which we will encounter at the end of the chapter;
    • lines 122–136: the [sansJournal] method executes an action without logging (SQL). It uses Logback’s API: each log ([Logger]) has a level, which can be modified during execution. We set the five logs to level [OFF], execute the action, and then restore the original levels in a [finally] clause, so that they remain at those levels even if the action throws an exception;
    • lines 139–141: [LoggerFactory] is the class of SLF4J that returns a log; Since Logback is the current implementation of SLF4J, the returned object is a [ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger].

    <?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!-- Logback configuration for the examples in this chapter -->
<configuration>

     <!-- the SQL compact log: formatted by the [outils.JournalSql] class -->
    <appender name="SQL" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder class="ch.qos.logback.core.encoder.LayoutWrappingEncoder">
            <layout class="outils.JournalSql"/>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

     <!-- other messages: level, log short name, text -->
    <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
        <encoder>
            <pattern>%-5level %logger{0} - %msg%n</pattern>
        </encoder>
    </appender>

     <!-- SQL commands (DEBUG), their parameters, transactions, batches (TRACE), and errors -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.SQL" level="DEBUG" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.resource.jdbc" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.batch" level="TRACE" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.error" level="WARN" additivity="false">
        <appender-ref ref="SQL"/>
    </logger>

     <!-- Hibernate’s built-in connection pool is sufficient for our examples: we suppress its warning -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.orm.connections.pooling" level="ERROR"/>

     <!-- Deleting tables from an empty database causes harmless errors: we suppress them -->
    <logger name="org.hibernate.tool.schema" level="OFF"/>

     <!-- all other logs: warnings and errors only -->
    <root level="WARN">
        <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
    </root>
</configuration>
    • lines 6–10: An “appender” writes the messages, in this case to the console. It uses our formatting;
    • lines 13–17: a second “appender” for the other messages: level, log short name, text;
    • lines 20–34: the Hibernate logs from the previous table, with their levels. Their messages go to the “appender” [SQL] and only to it ([additivity="false"]: they are not additionally forwarded to the root log);
    • line 37: the warning about Hibernate’s built-in connection pool is suppressed;
    • line 40: Hibernate deletes tables starting with their foreign keys; on an empty database, these deletions fail without consequence, but Hibernate logs this at length. These messages are suppressed;
    • lines 43–45: The other logs record only warnings and errors.

    The [outils] module has only one dependency: Logback. A library does not typically impose its logging configuration on the applications that use it; we do so here to avoid repeating this file in every example.

    package articles;

import jakarta.persistence.Column;
import jakarta.persistence.Entity;
import jakarta.persistence.GeneratedValue;
import jakarta.persistence.GenerationType;
import jakarta.persistence.Id;
import jakarta.persistence.Table;
import jakarta.persistence.UniqueConstraint;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

// A store item, with annotations specifying its table
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles",
        uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(name = "uk_articles_nom", columnNames = "nom"))
public class Article {

     // primary key, generated by SGBD (AUTO_INCREMENT)
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

     // item name: required, up to 30 characters, unique (see @Table)
    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String nom;

     // Price: 10 digits, including 2 decimal places
    @Column(nullable = false, precision = 10, scale = 2)
    private BigDecimal prix;

     // current stock and minimum stock level below which restocking is required
    private int stockActuel;
    private int stockMinimum;

     // the constructor without any parameters required by Hibernate (it may be protected)
    protected Article() {
    }
    • Lines 14–15: The table is named [articles], as in Chapter 10. The parameter [uniqueConstraints] declares a uniqueness constraint, named [uk_articles_nom], on the column [nom]: no two items can have the same name. Without an explicit name, Hibernate would generate an unreadable one ([UK3f8k...]), which would appear in error messages;
    • lines 24–25: a required name of no more than 30 characters;
    • lines 28–29: a price in [decimal(10,2)].

    package articles;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import outils.JournalSql;

// the database [hbarticles]: Hibernate configuration and database initialization
public final class BaseArticles {

     // the database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist (createDatabaseIfNotExist)
    public static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbarticles?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true";
    public static final String UTILISATEUR = "root";
    public static final String MOT_DE_PASSE = "";

     // utility class: no instance
    private BaseArticles() {
    }

     // Hibernate configuration: entities, database, formatting of the SQL log
    public static HibernatePersistenceConfiguration configuration() {
        return new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("articles")
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                .jdbcUrl(URL)
                .jdbcCredentials(UTILISATEUR, MOT_DE_PASSE)
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true);
    }

     // a SessionFactory for the [hbarticles] database, using the previous configuration
    public static SessionFactory creerSessionFactory() {
        return configuration().createEntityManagerFactory();
    }

     // (re)creation of the table [articles] with its six items, without the log SQL
    public static void initialiser(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        JournalSql.sansJournal(() -> {
             // deletion and subsequent creation of the entity tables
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
             // the six items, added in a single transaction
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                session.persist(new Article("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), 10, 5));
                session.persist(new Article("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(10), 10, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("arc", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), 4, 1));
                session.persist(new Article("flèches - lot de 6", BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 12, 20));
                session.persist(new Article("combinaison de plongée", BigDecimal.valueOf(300), 8, 2));
                session.persist(new Article("bouteilles d'oxygène", BigDecimal.valueOf(120), 10, 5));
            });
        });
    }
}
    • lines 13–15: the database’s URL and the user, both public so that other modules can use them;
    • lines 22–28: the Hibernate configuration. It is returned by a public method, which will allow an instance to complete it before creating the [SessionFactory]. The [FORMAT_SQL] property ([hibernate.format_sql]) instructs Hibernate to format the SQL, which it then passes to the [org.hibernate.SQL] log: it is this formatted data that the [JournalSql] class then condenses;
    • lines 31–33: the [SessionFactory] from the [hbarticles] database;
    • lines 36–51: a method that recreates the table [articles] with its six items, without the log SQL: we do not want to see the SQL from this initialization in the example results;
    • line 42: [sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> ...)] opens a session, starts a transaction, executes the lambda (Chapter 7) by passing it the session, commits the transaction (or rolls it back if the lambda throws an exception), and closes the session. This is the shortest way to write a work unit; we’ll use it often, along with its variants [inSession] (a session without a transaction), [fromTransaction], and [fromSession] (which return the result of the lambda).

    11.4.3. Other Ways to Configure Hibernate

    We configure Hibernate programmatically using [HibernatePersistenceConfiguration]. There are other ways to do this, which can be found in applications and documentation:

    • a [META-INF/persistence.xml] file, the traditional approach used by Jakarta Persistence: it describes one or more persistence units (entity classes, connection properties, options), and the factory is created using [Persistence.createEntityManagerFactory("articles")];
    • a [hibernate.properties] (or [hibernate.cfg.xml]) file, specific to Hibernate, read by the [org.hibernate.cfg.Configuration] class: [new Configuration().addAnnotatedClass(Article.class).buildSessionFactory()]. This is the approach used in older versions of Hibernate;
    • in a Spring Boot application, the properties [spring.datasource.*] and [spring.jpa.*] from the file [application.properties]: Spring Boot creates the factory itself.

    The properties are the same everywhere ([hibernate.format_sql], [jakarta.persistence.jdbc.url]...): only the way they are specified changes.

    11.5. Basic operations: add, read, update, delete

    11.5.1. The [crud] program

    The [crud] module demonstrates the four basic operations (CRUD: Create, Read, Update, Delete), as well as entity tracking via the session. To make this tracking visible, it uses a few internal Hibernate methods (its “SPI,” Service Provider Interface), intended for Hibernate extensions rather than applications: they are grouped in the utility methods at the end of the program.

    package crud;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Objects;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.EntityEntry;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.PersistenceContext;
import org.hibernate.engine.spi.SessionImplementor;
import org.hibernate.persister.entity.EntityPersister;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six records
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                 // 1 - search by primary key
                IO.println("--- find(1)");
                Article velo = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println(velo);
                IO.println("--- find(1) une seconde fois");
                Article velo2 = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println("même objet : " + (velo == velo2));

                 // 2 - Add an item
                IO.println("--- persist");
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article x = new Article("x", BigDecimal.valueOf(100), 10, 1);
                IO.println("avant persist : état=" + etat(session, x) + ", id=" + x.getId());
                session.persist(x);
                IO.println("après persist : état=" + etat(session, x) + ", id=" + x.getId());
                transaction.commit();

                 // 3 - Update: simply modify the object
                IO.println("--- modification du prix");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                x.setPrix(x.getPrix().multiply(new BigDecimal("1.1")));
                IO.println("session modifiée : %s, prix d'origine=%s, prix actuel=%s"
                        .formatted(session.isDirty(), valeurOrigine(session, x, "prix"), x.getPrix()));
                IO.println("--- commit");
                transaction.commit();
                IO.println("après commit : session modifiée : " + session.isDirty());

                 // 4 - deletion
                IO.println("--- remove");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                session.remove(x);
                IO.println("avant commit : état=" + etat(session, x));
                transaction.commit();
                IO.println("après commit : état=" + etat(session, x));

                 // 5 - an object detached, modified, and then merged with the session
                IO.println("--- detach et merge");
                Article arc = session.find(Article.class, 3);
                session.detach(arc);
                IO.println("après detach : état=" + etat(session, arc));
                arc.setPrix(BigDecimal.valueOf(550));
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article arcGere = session.merge(arc);
                IO.println("merge : même objet=%s, état de l'objet rendu=%s"
                        .formatted(arc == arcGere, etat(session, arcGere)));
                transaction.commit();

                 // 6 - Entities tracked by the session
                IO.println("--- les entités suivies");
                velo.setStockActuel(velo.getStockActuel() - 1);
                afficherEntitesSuivies(session);
            }
        }
    }

     // the status of an item relative to the session (Hibernate’s internal API)
    private static String etat(Session session, Article article) {
        EntityEntry entree = contexte(session).getEntry(article);
        if (entree != null) {
             // MANAGED, DELETED...
            return entree.getStatus().name();
        }
         // an object unknown to the session: never saved (no ID) or detached
        return article.getId() == null ? "TRANSIENT" : "DETACHED";
    }

     // the value of a property as read from the database (Hibernate's internal API)
    private static Object valeurOrigine(Session session, Object entite, String propriete) {
        return contexte(session).getEntry(entite).getLoadedValue(propriete);
    }

     // entities in the session's persistence context (Hibernate's internal API)
    private static void afficherEntitesSuivies(Session session) {
        for (Map.Entry<Object, EntityEntry> paire : contexte(session).reentrantSafeEntityEntries()) {
            EntityEntry entree = paire.getValue();
            EntityPersister persister = entree.getPersister();
            IO.println("%s #%s %s".formatted(persister.getEntityName(), entree.getId(), entree.getStatus()));
             // current property values, compared to the values read from the database
            String[] noms = persister.getPropertyNames();
            Object[] actuelles = persister.getValues(paire.getKey());
            Object[] origines = entree.getLoadedState();
            for (int i = 0; i < noms.length; i++) {
                String modification = Objects.equals(actuelles[i], origines[i]) ? ""
                        : " (modifiée, valeur d'origine : " + origines[i] + ")";
                IO.println("    %s : %s%s".formatted(noms[i], actuelles[i], modification));
            }
        }
        IO.println("session modifiée : " + session.isDirty());
    }

     // the session persistence context (Hibernate's internal API)
    private static PersistenceContext contexte(Session session) {
        return session.unwrap(SessionImplementor.class).getPersistenceContext();
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Line 25: [session.find(Article.class, 1)] searches for the primary key entry 1. It returns [null] if the key does not exist. The generated SQL (lines 3–6 of the results) is a configured [SELECT], whose parameter is set to 1: the compact log now displays the parameter values;
    • line 28: the second call to [find(Article.class, 1)] does not send any SQL commands and returns the same object (line 9). The session stores the entities it has read or saved in its persistence context—also known as the first-level cache: before querying the database, [find] checks to see if the requested entity is already there. A session never contains two objects for the same row in the database;
    • Lines 34–37: adding an item. Before [persist], the object is [TRANSIENT] (“transient”): the session does not recognize it, and its identifier is [null] (line 12). [persist] brings it into the session, which immediately executes the command [INSERT] (lines 13–18) to obtain the generated key and places it in the field [id]. The item is then [MANAGED] (“managed” or “persistent”) and its identifier is 7 (line 19). The transaction is opened on line 33 and committed on line 38 (lines 11 and 20 of the results);
    • line 43: To modify a row in the database, simply modify the object. No [update] method is required: the session has retained a copy of the values read or saved (the original state) and compares the current values to those. This is known as “dirty checking”;
    • lines 44–45: [session.isDirty()] indicates whether the session contains changes that have not yet been committed to the database: this is the case (line 23). The method [valeurOrigine] (lines 90–92) reads the original price value, 100, from the persistence context, whereas the current value is 110.0;
    • line 47: [commit] synchronizes the session with the database (“flush”): the [UPDATE] command is executed (lines 25–32), and then the transaction is committed. After that, the session has no pending changes (line 34);
    • Note that the [UPDATE] command writes all columns in the table, not just the one that has changed. This is Hibernate’s default behavior: a single SQL command, prepared once and for all, is used for all article modifications. In contrast, the [@DynamicUpdate] annotation placed on the entity instructs it to generate a query limited to the modified columns each time;
    • Lines 53–56: deletion. [remove] changes the article’s status to [DELETED] (line 37); [commit] sends the command [DELETE] (lines 38–40). The object is then no longer recognized by the session: it becomes [DETACHED] (“detached,” line 42);
    • lines 60–63: the arc is read (lines 44–47), then detached from the session by [detach]: the session forgets it (line 48). Any change to its price is then ignored. A detached object is a common occurrence in an application: it is an object read by a session that is now closed—for example, during a previous HTTP query—and subsequently modified by the user;
    • line 65: [session.merge(arc)] merges the detached object with the session. The session reads the record from the database (lines 50–53), copies the state of the detached object into the entity it manages, and returns the latter: this is not the same object (line 54). The object passed to [merge] remains detached; the returned object is the one that must be used next. [commit] saves the new price (lines 55–62);
    • line 72: the bike’s inventory is updated, without saving;
    • lines 95–111: display of the persistence context. For each tracked entity ([EntityEntry]), its name, ID, and status are displayed, followed by the current value of each property and its original value if different. The [EntityPersister] object is the one in Hibernate that knows the mapping between an entity and its table: it provides the names of the properties and their values;
    • Lines 65–75 of the results: the session tracks the bike, whose inventory has changed from 10 to 9, and the arc. The change to the bike is not saved: the session is closed without synchronization. There is no [commit], and a session does not synchronize automatically upon closure.

    11.5.2. The States of an Entity

    An entity is, with respect to a session, in one of the following states (Jakarta Persistence refers to them as “new,” “managed,” “detached,” and “removed”):

    State
    Meaning
    transient ([TRANSIENT])
    The object was created by [new] and has never been saved: it has no ID, and no session recognizes it
    managed ([MANAGED])
    The object has been read or saved by the session, which is tracking it: changes to it will be reflected in the database during the next synchronization
    Deleted ([DELETED])
    The object has been marked for deletion ([remove]): the next synchronization will send the command [DELETE]
    detached ([DETACHED])
    The object corresponds to a row in the database, but the session that read it is closed or has forgotten it ([detach], [clear]): its changes are ignored unless it is merged with a session ([merge])

    The session synchronization (“flush”) sends the SQL commands to SGBD, which propagate the changes to the managed entities. This occurs:

    • during the [commit] phase of the transaction;
    • before executing a query whose result might depend on changes that have not yet been committed ([FlushMode.AUTO] mode, the default mode): the query thus sees the session data;
    • during an explicit call to [session.flush()]. The commands are then executed, but they will not be permanently committed until the transaction’s [commit].

    Here’s an overview of the workflow with Hibernate: we open a session and a transaction, read entities, modify them as ordinary objects, add them ([persist]), and delete them ([remove]), then commit the transaction, which sends all necessary commands to the database in a single batch. The session acts as a “unit of work.” It is a lightweight object designed for a short lifespan: a unit of work, such as a HTTP query in a web application. You do not use the same session throughout the entire life of an application; otherwise, it would accumulate the tracked entities in its persistence context.

    11.6. The requests HQL

    11.6.1. HQL and JPQL

    To retrieve entities other than by their primary key, queries are written in a language similar to SQL, but one that refers to entities and attributes rather than tables and columns: HQL (Hibernate Query Language). Jakarta Persistence defines a similar language, JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language), of which HQL is a superset: a JPQL query is a valid HQL query. Hibernate translates the query into SQL, in the SGBD dialect, and SGBD executes it.

    Some differences from SQL:

    • We use the entity name ([Article]), not the table name ([articles]), and the attribute names ([stockActuel]), not the column names. Entity and attribute names are case-sensitive, just like in Java;
    • the clause [select] is optional in HQL: [from Article] returns entities [Article]. JPQL requires writing [select a from Article a];
    • relationships between entities are traversed using a dot ([p.categorie.nom]), with Hibernate writing the joins itself, as we will see.

    A query is created by the session’s [createSelectionQuery] method (Hibernate 6), which takes the text HQL and the result type as arguments, and returns a [SelectionQuery<T>] object. You can then set its parameters and execute it with [getResultList] (a list), [getSingleResult] (a single result; an exception if there are zero or more), [getSingleResultOrNull] ([null] if there are none), or [getResultStream] (a stream). The Jakarta Persistence method [createQuery] also exists; it is used for both read queries and updates.

    package hql;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.query.SemanticException;

public class Main {

     // a projection: the name of an item and its inventory value
    record ValeurStock(String nom, BigDecimal valeur) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                 // 1 - filtering and sorting
                IO.println("--- les articles à réapprovisionner, par ordre alphabétique");
                String hql = "from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum order by nom";
                List<Article> aCommander = session.createSelectionQuery(hql, Article.class).getResultList();
                aCommander.forEach(IO::println);

                 // 2 - projection: only the relevant columns are retrieved
                IO.println("--- valeur du stock de chaque article");
                List<ValeurStock> valeurs = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select nom, prix * stockActuel from Article
                                order by prix * stockActuel desc""", ValeurStock.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (ValeurStock v : valeurs) {
                    IO.println("%s : %.2f euros".formatted(v.nom(), v.valeur()));
                }

                 // 3 - a single result; the value [prixMin] is passed via a named parameter
                IO.println("--- le premier article de plus de 200 euros");
                BigDecimal prixMin = BigDecimal.valueOf(200);
                Article article = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select a from Article a
                                where a.prix > :prixMin order by a.prix""", Article.class)
                        .setParameter("prixMin", prixMin)
                        .setMaxResults(1)
                        .getSingleResultOrNull();
                IO.println(article == null ? "aucun" : article);

                 // 4 - aggregates: the calculation is performed by SGBD
                IO.println("--- agrégats");
                long nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery("select count(*) from Article", Long.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                BigDecimal valeurStock = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("select sum(prix * stockActuel) from Article", BigDecimal.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println("%d articles, valeur du stock : %.2f euros".formatted(nbArticles, valeurStock));

                 // 5 - `LIKE` and `IN`; a Java list as the value of a parameter
                IO.println("--- like et in");
                List<String> noms = List.of("arc", "pompe", "raquette");
                List<String> resultats = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("""
                                select nom from Article
                                where nom like 'b%' or nom in :noms""", String.class)
                        .setParameter("noms", noms)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println(String.join(", ", resultats));

                 // 6 - pagination: the third page of two items, sorted by price in ascending order
                IO.println("--- pagination");
                int taillePage = 2, numeroPage = 3;
                List<Article> page = session.createSelectionQuery("from Article order by prix", Article.class)
                        .setFirstResult((numeroPage - 1) * taillePage)
                        .setMaxResults(taillePage)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println("page %d : %s".formatted(numeroPage, page.stream()
                        .map(a -> "%s (%.2f euros)".formatted(a.getNom(), a.getPrix()))
                        .collect(Collectors.joining(", "))));

                 // 7 - An invalid query is rejected as soon as it is created, before execution
                IO.println("--- requête incorrecte");
                try {
                    session.createSelectionQuery("from Article where stock < stockMinimum", Article.class);
                } catch (SemanticException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
                }

                 // 8 - A rule written in Java cannot be translated into SQL: in-memory filtering
                IO.println("--- filtrage en mémoire");
                try (Stream<Article> flux = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article", Article.class)
                        .getResultStream()) {
                    flux.filter(Regles::enRupture).forEach(IO::println);
                }
            }
        }
    }

     // A business rule written in Java
    static final class Regles {

        private Regles() {
        }

         // An item is out of stock if its inventory is below the minimum stock level
        static boolean enRupture(Article a) {
            return a.getStockActuel() < a.getStockMinimum();
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 26–27: The clause [where] compares two attributes of the entity; the [order by] clause sorts by name: they become the [WHERE] and [ORDER BY] clauses in the SQL sequence (lines 5–6). The query is executed by [getResultList];
    • lines 32–36: a projection. The query does not return entities, but rather two values per item: the name and the stock value. The generated SQL (line 9) requests only the necessary columns and performs the calculation itself. The result type is the [ValeurStock] record in lines 16–17: Hibernate creates one record per line, passing the values from the [select] clause to its constructor in order. These objects are not entities: the session does not track them. The query is written in a text block (Java 15, Chapter 3), which is more readable than a long string;
    • lines 44–50: a query written as in JPQL, with an alias ([a]). [:prixMin] is a named parameter, whose value is given by [setParameter]. It becomes a parameter of the command SQL (line 21): therefore, we do not need to worry about SQL injections, since the value is transmitted separately from the command text. This is the rule that Chapter 10 applied to prepared queries. [setMaxResults(1)] limits the result to one row: the clause [LIMIT] of MySQL (line 23). A literal value written in the query text (such as ['b%'] on line 68: line 36 of the results) is, on the other hand, copied into the order text SQL: values coming from outside the program must always be passed as parameters;
    • Lines 55–59: The aggregates [count] and [sum] are calculated by SGBD (lines 28–31): only the result is transferred, not the rows. HQL also references [avg], [min], [max], and the clauses [group by] and [having];
    • lines 65–70: the operator [like] of SQL, and the operator [in], whose operand is a parameter that receives a Java list: Hibernate expands it into as many SQL parameters as there are elements in the list (line 36). HQL supports numerous functions on strings ([upper], [length], [substring]...), dates, and numbers, which it translates into the SGBD dialect;
    • lines 76–79: pagination, to display a long list page by page. [setFirstResult] skips the entries from the previous pages, while [setMaxResults] keeps those from the requested page: the [LIMIT ?, ?] clause of MySQL (lines 45–47). Pagination only makes sense on a sorted list ([order by]). Lines 80–82 construct the page display using a stream and [Collectors.joining] (Chapter 5);
    • lines 86–90: a query that uses an attribute [stock] that does not exist. The error is detected as soon as the query is created, before any execution, because Hibernate parses the text HQL and compares it to the model: it throws a [SemanticException] (line 50; Hibernate messages are in English). A syntax error would result in a [SyntaxException];
    • lines 94–98: a query cannot use a Java method, such as [Regles.enRupture] (lines 110–112): Hibernate does not know the code, and even if it did, it would not necessarily know how to write it in SQL. You can read all entities and filter them in memory using the API Stream: [getResultStream] returns a [Stream<Article>] (which must be closed after use, hence the [try] statement with resources). The result is correct (line 54), but the entire table was transferred (lines 52–53): with a large table, this should be avoided. It is better to include the condition in the query, as shown on line 26.

    11.6.3. Named Queries and Compile-Time Validation

    A query written in a string is only parsed at runtime. There are two ways to detect errors earlier:

    • named queries: the annotation ***[@NamedQuery(name = "Article.enRupture", query = "from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum")]***, placed on the entity, declares a query that Hibernate parses at startup, when creating the *[SessionFactory]*. It is then executed by its name: [session.createNamedSelectionQuery("Article.enRupture", Article.class)];
    • the Hibernate annotation processor ("Hibernate Processor," library [org.hibernate.orm:hibernate-processor]), declared in the compiler configuration ([annotationProcessorPaths] derived from [maven-compiler-plugin]). Executed by [javac] during compilation, it checks annotation requests and generates, for each entity, a “metamodel” class " class ([Article_] for [Article]), which we will encounter again with the API Criteria. We do not use it in this course.

    11.7. The API Criteria

    11.7.1. Queries built using code

    A HQL query is a string that can be constructed by concatenation: this is unreliable and hard to read as soon as the query depends on many optional criteria (a search form, for example). Jakarta Persistence offers another way to write queries: API Criteria, where the query is a tree of objects constructed through method calls. Hibernate translates this tree into SQL, just as it does with a HQL query (it also translates HQL into such a tree). The [criteria] module reuses several queries from the previous program:
