    package criteria;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.CriteriaQuery;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Expression;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Predicate;
import jakarta.persistence.criteria.Root;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.query.criteria.HibernateCriteriaBuilder;

public class Main {

     // a projection: the name of an item and its stock value
    record ValeurStock(String nom, BigDecimal valeur) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                 // Generating query elements
                HibernateCriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();

                 // 1 - filtering and sorting
                IO.println("--- les articles à réapprovisionner, par ordre alphabétique");
                CriteriaQuery<Article> requete = cb.createQuery(Article.class);
                Root<Article> a = requete.from(Article.class);
                requete.select(a)
                        .where(cb.lt(a.<Integer>get("stockActuel"), a.<Integer>get("stockMinimum")))
                        .orderBy(cb.asc(a.get("nom")));
                session.createSelectionQuery(requete).getResultList().forEach(IO::println);

                 // 2 - Projection to a single record
                IO.println("--- valeur du stock de chaque article");
                CriteriaQuery<ValeurStock> projection = cb.createQuery(ValeurStock.class);
                Root<Article> p = projection.from(Article.class);
                Expression<BigDecimal> valeur = cb
                        .prod(p.<BigDecimal>get("prix"), p.<Integer>get("stockActuel"))
                        .as(BigDecimal.class);
                projection.select(cb.construct(ValeurStock.class, p.get("nom"), valeur))
                        .orderBy(cb.desc(valeur));
                for (ValeurStock v : session.createSelectionQuery(projection).getResultList()) {
                    IO.println("%s : %.2f euros".formatted(v.nom(), v.valeur()));
                }

                 // 3 - a query built according to the provided criteria
                IO.println("--- recherche : prix maximal 150 euros");
                rechercher(session, BigDecimal.valueOf(150), null).forEach(IO::println);
                IO.println("--- recherche : prix maximal 150 euros et nom commençant par [b]");
                rechercher(session, BigDecimal.valueOf(150), "b").forEach(IO::println);

                 // 4 - Aggregates
                IO.println("--- agrégats");
                CriteriaQuery<Long> compte = cb.createQuery(Long.class);
                compte.select(cb.count(compte.from(Article.class)));
                long nbArticles = session.createSelectionQuery(compte).getSingleResult();
                CriteriaQuery<BigDecimal> somme = cb.createQuery(BigDecimal.class);
                Root<Article> s = somme.from(Article.class);
                somme.select(cb.sum(cb
                        .prod(s.<BigDecimal>get("prix"), s.<Integer>get("stockActuel"))
                        .as(BigDecimal.class)));
                BigDecimal valeurStock = session.createSelectionQuery(somme).getSingleResult();
                IO.println("%d articles, valeur du stock : %.2f euros".formatted(nbArticles, valeurStock));
            }
        }
    }

     // items whose price does not exceed [prixMax] and whose name begins with [debutNom],
     // each criterion is used only if it is not null
    static List<Article> rechercher(Session session, BigDecimal prixMax, String debutNom) {
        HibernateCriteriaBuilder cb = session.getCriteriaBuilder();
        CriteriaQuery<Article> requete = cb.createQuery(Article.class);
        Root<Article> a = requete.from(Article.class);
         // the conditions, added one by one
        List<Predicate> conditions = new ArrayList<>();
        if (prixMax != null) {
            conditions.add(cb.le(a.get("prix"), prixMax));
        }
        if (debutNom != null) {
            conditions.add(cb.like(a.get("nom"), debutNom + "%"));
        }
        requete.select(a).where(conditions.toArray(Predicate[]::new)).orderBy(cb.asc(a.get("prix")));
        return session.createSelectionQuery(requete).getResultList();
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 28: the session returns a [HibernateCriteriaBuilder], the Hibernate-enhanced version of Jakarta Persistence’s [CriteriaBuilder]: this is the factory for all elements of a query (conditions, expressions, sorts);
    • Lines 32–36: The query from the first example, HQL. [createQuery(Article.class)] creates a query that returns articles; [from(Article.class)] declares the queried entity and returns its root ([Root<Article>]), which is the equivalent of the alias [a] for [from Article a]; [a.get("stockActuel")] designates an attribute. The condition is constructed by [cb.lt(x, y)] (“less than,” [x < y]), and the sort by [cb.asc(...)]. The notation [a.<Integer>get(...)] provides the compiler with the attribute’s type, which the string ["stockActuel"] does not allow it to determine;
    • line 37: the query is executed by the session as a HQL query. The generated SQL (lines 3–6) is the same as that of the HQL query;
    • Lines 41–47: a projection onto the record [ValeurStock]. [cb.prod(x, y)] is the product of two expressions; [as(BigDecimal.class)] specifies the result type; [cb.construct(ValeurStock.class, ...)] indicates that each row of the result must be passed to the record constructor;
    • Lines 76–90: This is where the API Criteria is most useful. The [rechercher] method constructs a query based on the criteria provided to it: each condition is added to the list of conditions only if the corresponding criterion is not [null], and the [where] clause receives all the conditions from the list, combined by [and]. The first call (line 54) produces a query with one condition (line 21), while the second (line 56) produces a query with two conditions (line 30). Note that with the API criteria, Hibernate passes the values ([150], [b%]) as parameters in the order SQL;
    • lines 60–68: the aggregates [count] and [sum].

    11.7.2. The static metamodel

    The weakness of these queries is that attributes are designated by strings ([a.get("stockActuel")]): a typo will not be detected until runtime, and the compiler ignores the attribute’s type. To address this, Jakarta Persistence provides a static metamodel: for each entity [Article], there is a class [Article_] that contains one field per attribute, describing its name and type. You then write ***[cb.lt(a.get(Article\_.stockActuel), a.get(Article\_.stockMinimum))]***, which the compiler fully validates. These classes are not written by hand: they are generated during compilation by the Hibernate annotation processor mentioned above. This is the recommended approach in a real-world project that uses API Criteria.

    For a fixed query, HQL is more readable than the API Criteria; for a query that is constructed based on the circumstances, the API Criteria is safer. The two can be combined: Hibernate allows you to create a Criteria query from a HQL ([cb.createQuery(hql, Article.class)]) string and then supplement it with code.

    11.8. Relationships

    11.8.1. The store model

    // a category includes multiple products (one-to-many relationship)
@Entity
@Table(name = "categories")
public class Categorie {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String nom;

     // Products in the category: the inverse side of the relationship, described by Produit.categorie
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "categorie", cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    private List<Produit> produits = new ArrayList<>();

    protected Categorie() {
    }

    public Categorie(String nom) {
        this.nom = nom;
    }

     // Adding a product: both sides of the relationship are updated
    public void ajouter(Produit produit) {
        produits.add(produit);
        produit.setCategorie(this);
    }

    public Integer getId() {
        return id;
    }

    public String getNom() {
        return nom;
    }

    public List<Produit> getProduits() {
        return produits;
    }
}

@Entity
@Table(name = "produits")
public class Produit {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)

    @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)
    @JoinColumn(name = "categorie_id", foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_categorie"))

    @ManyToMany(cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST)
    @JoinTable(name = "produits_etiquettes",
            joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "produit_id"),
            inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "etiquette_id"),
            foreignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_etiquettes_produit"),
            inverseForeignKey = @ForeignKey(name = "fk_produits_etiquettes_etiquette"))

    protected Produit() {
    }

    public Produit(String nom, BigDecimal prix, Etiquette... etiquettes) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.prix = prix;
         // only the owner side of the relationship is populated: this is the one Hibernate stores
        this.etiquettes.addAll(List.of(etiquettes));
    }

    It contains the three types of associations:

    • a many-to-one relationship ([@ManyToOne]): a product belongs to a category (Product, lines 17–19). In the database, this is represented by a foreign key, the column [categorie_id] in the table [produits], where [@JoinColumn] provides the name and the constraint name ([fk_produits_categorie]). [optional = false] enforces the relationship: the column will be [NOT NULL];
    • the inverse, one-to-many relationship ([@OneToMany]): a category contains multiple products (Category, lines 14–15). It does not create anything in the database: [mappedBy = "categorie"] indicates that it is described by the field [categorie] of the entity [Produit]. [Produit.categorie] is said to be the owner side of the relationship, and [Categorie.produits] its inverse side: Hibernate saves the value of the owner side. However, both sides must be kept consistent in memory: this is the role of the [ajouter] method (Category, lines 25–28), which adds the product to the list and sets its category;
    • a many-to-many relationship ([@ManyToMany]): a product has multiple labels, and a label is associated with multiple products. It is stored in an association table, [produits_etiquettes], whose name, the names of the two columns, and the names of the two foreign keys are provided by [@JoinTable] (Product, lines 22–28). The reverse side is [Etiquette.produits] ([mappedBy = "etiquettes"]). For a many-to-many relationship, a [Set] is preferred over a [List]: with a list, Hibernate deletes and re-inserts all rows in the association table every time the collection is modified;
    • [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] specifies lazy loading of a product’s category: it will only be read when it is used. This is the default behavior for collections ([@OneToMany], [@ManyToMany]), but not for relationships to a single entity ([@ManyToOne]), which the standard loads immediately by default ([EAGER]): [fetch = FetchType.LAZY] is systematically added to them, as recommended by the Hibernate documentation;
    • [cascade = CascadeType.PERSIST] propagates the operation [persist]: persisting a category persists its products, and persisting a product persists its tags. The other values ([MERGE], [REMOVE], [ALL]...) propagate the other operations;
    • Collections are initialized with an empty collection, and the field of a relationship to a single entity remains [null] until it has been populated. The methods [setCategorie], [setClient], and [setCommande] are not public: only the methods [ajouter] in the same package call them.

    package relations;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import outils.JournalSql;

// the database [hbboutique]: Hibernate configuration and first dataset
public final class Boutique {

    private Boutique() {
    }

     // a SessionFactory for the database [hbboutique] and its six entities
    public static SessionFactory creerSessionFactory() {
        return new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("boutique")
                .managedClasses(Categorie.class, Produit.class, Etiquette.class,
                        Client.class, Commande.class, LigneCommande.class)
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbboutique?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory();
    }

     // (re)creation of tables and an initial dataset, without a log SQL
    public static void initialiser(SessionFactory sessionFactory) {
        JournalSql.sansJournal(() -> {
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
            sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                 // two labels
                Etiquette promo = new Etiquette("promo");
                Etiquette nouveaute = new Etiquette("nouveauté");
                 // three categories and their products: an object graph
                Categorie cycles = new Categorie("cycles");
                cycles.ajouter(new Produit("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(500), promo));
                Produit pompe = new Produit("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(10));
                cycles.ajouter(pompe);
                Categorie tirALArc = new Categorie("tir à l'arc");
                Produit arc = new Produit("arc", BigDecimal.valueOf(600), nouveaute);
                tirALArc.ajouter(arc);
                tirALArc.ajouter(new Produit("flèches - lot de 6", BigDecimal.valueOf(100),
                        promo, nouveaute));
                Categorie plongee = new Categorie("plongée");
                 // Persistence propagates to products and labels (cascade)
                session.persist(cycles);
                session.persist(tirALArc);
                session.persist(plongee);
                 // a customer and their two-line order
                Commande commande = new Commande(LocalDate.of(2026, 9, 28));
                commande.ajouter(new LigneCommande(pompe, 2));
                commande.ajouter(new LigneCommande(arc, 1));
                Client martin = new Client("Martin");
                martin.ajouter(commande);
                session.persist(martin);
            });
        });
    }
}
    • lines 19–20: the six entities, declared by [managedClasses];
    • lines 34–46: an object graph: three categories, their products, and the products’ labels;
    • lines 48–50: it is sufficient to persist the categories: thanks to cascading, Hibernate traverses the associations and persists all the entities it reaches, in the correct order (the categories before the products that reference them), populating the foreign keys and the association table;
    • lines 52–57: a customer, their order, and its two line items, persisted in a single operation.

    package relations;

import jakarta.persistence.EntityGraph;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import org.hibernate.LazyInitializationException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

     // the results of the projection queries
    record ProduitCategorie(String produit, String categorie) {
    }

    record MontantCommande(Integer id, String client, BigDecimal montant) {
    }

    record StatistiquesCategorie(String categorie, Long nombre, Double prixMoyen) {
    }

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = Boutique.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // 1 - Creating tables and an initial dataset, without a log
            Boutique.initialiser(sessionFactory);

             // 2 - a customer, their order, and its lines, added all at once
            IO.println("--- ajout d'un client, d'une commande et de ses deux lignes");
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                Produit velo = produit(session, "vélo");
                Produit fleches = produit(session, "flèches - lot de 6");
                Commande commande = new Commande(LocalDate.of(2026, 10, 1));
                commande.ajouter(new LigneCommande(velo, 1));
                commande.ajouter(new LigneCommande(fleches, 3));
                Client client = new Client("Dupont");
                client.ajouter(commande);
                session.persist(client);
                IO.println("client n° %d, commande n° %d".formatted(client.getId(), commande.getId()));
            });

             // 3 - Lazy loading: relations are read on demand
            IO.println("--- chargement paresseux");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                List<Commande> commandes = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Commande order by id", Commande.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Commande commande : commandes) {
                    IO.println("commande n° %d : client=%s, %d ligne(s)".formatted(commande.getId(),
                            commande.getClient().getNom(), commande.getLignes().size()));
                }
            });

             // 4 - An unloaded relation is no longer accessible once the session is closed
            IO.println("--- après la fermeture de la session");
            Commande commandeDetachee = sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s.find(Commande.class, 1));
            try {
                IO.println(commandeDetachee.getLignes().size() + " ligne(s)");
            } catch (LazyInitializationException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }

             // 5 - join fetch: orders, their customers, their line items, and their products in a single query
            IO.println("--- join fetch");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                List<Commande> commandes = session.createSelectionQuery("""
                        from Commande c
                        join fetch c.client
                        join fetch c.lignes l
                        join fetch l.produit
                        order by c.id""", Commande.class).getResultList();
                for (Commande commande : commandes) {
                    IO.println("commande n° %d du %s pour %s".formatted(commande.getId(), commande.getDate(),
                            commande.getClient().getNom()));
                    for (LigneCommande ligne : commande.getLignes()) {
                        Produit produit = ligne.getProduit();
                        IO.println("  %d x %s à %.2f euros"
                                .formatted(ligne.getQuantite(), produit.getNom(), produit.getPrix()));
                    }
                }
            });

             // 6 - An entity graph: what to load with the entity, described outside the query
            IO.println("--- graphe d'entités");
            Categorie categorie = sessionFactory.fromSession(session -> {
                EntityGraph<Categorie> graphe = session.createEntityGraph(Categorie.class);
                graphe.addAttributeNode("produits");
                return session.find(graphe, 2);
            });
             // The session is closed, but the products have been loaded
            IO.println("%s : %s".formatted(categorie.getNom(),
                    categorie.getProduits().stream().map(Produit::getNom).collect(Collectors.joining(", "))));

             // 7 - The many-to-many relationship in a single query
            IO.println("--- les produits en promotion");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select p.nom, p.categorie.nom from Produit p join p.etiquettes e
                            where e.libelle = 'promo' order by p.nom""", ProduitCategorie.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(p -> IO.println("%s (%s)".formatted(p.produit(), p.categorie()))));

             // 8 - a calculation across relationships, performed by SGBD
            IO.println("--- montant des commandes");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select c.id, c.client.nom, sum(l.quantite * l.produit.prix)
                            from Commande c join c.lignes l
                            group by c.id, c.client.nom order by c.id""", MontantCommande.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(m -> IO.println("commande n° %d (%s) : %.2f euros"
                            .formatted(m.id(), m.client(), m.montant()))));

             // 9 - a grouping: number of products and average price by category
            IO.println("--- produits par catégorie");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session.createSelectionQuery("""
                            select p.categorie.nom, count(*), avg(p.prix) from Produit p
                            group by p.categorie.nom order by p.categorie.nom""", StatistiquesCategorie.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(s -> IO.println("%s : %d produit(s), prix moyen %.2f euros".formatted(
                            s.categorie(), s.nombre(), s.prixMoyen()))));
        }
    }

     // the product with the given name
    private static Produit produit(Session session, String nom) {
        return session.createSelectionQuery("from Produit where nom = :nom", Produit.class)
                .setParameter("nom", nom)
                .getSingleResult();
    }
}

    Comments:

    • lines 15–22: the records that will receive the projection results;
    • lines 32–39: the output is read by the [produit] method (lines 125–129); a customer, their order, and its two lines are persisted with a single call to [persist]. SQL (lines 12–28 of the results) shows the order of insertions: the customer, then the order, whose foreign key [client_id] receives the key generated for the customer (2), then the rows, whose foreign key [commande_id] receives the key from the order;
    • Lines 46–52: lazy loading. The query reads only the orders (lines 32–34): the customer and the lines for each order are read only when the program uses them, via additional queries (lines 35–42 for the first order, 44–51 for the second). For the client, Hibernate has placed a proxy in the [client] field—an object of a subclass of [Client] generated by Hibernate (using Byte Buddy)—which contains only the identifier and loads the client upon the first call to a method ([getNom()]). This is why an entity must not be a [final] class. For the rows, the list is a Hibernate collection, loaded upon its first use ([size()]);
    • Lines 57–62: The command is read by a session that is immediately closed ([fromSession]). These rows were not loaded, and once the session is closed, they can no longer be loaded: accessing the collection triggers a [LazyInitializationException] (line 58), one of the most common exceptions in applications that use Hibernate. You must load what you need while the session is open;
    • Lines 67–72: preloading via a query. [join fetch] instructs Hibernate to load, along with the orders, their customers, their lines, and the product of each line: a single query with joins (lines 60–78). The display shows the two orders and their line items (lines 79–84). The join with the line items produces one SQL record per order line; Hibernate derives a single order for each identifier: the rendered list does indeed contain two orders;
    • lines 86–90: an “entity graph” (Jakarta Persistence) describes, independently of any query, the associations to be loaded with an entity: in this case, the products in the category. [session.find(graphe, 2)] (Jakarta Persistence 3.2) retrieves category 2 along with its products in a single query (lines 86–90 of the results). Once the session is closed, the products remain accessible (lines 92–93). To load an association later, while the session is open, we write [Hibernate.initialize(categorie.getProduits())];
    • Lines 97–101: associations are used in queries: [join p.etiquettes e] traverses the many-to-many relationship (two joins, with the association table and the label table, lines 95–96), and [p.categorie.nom] is translated into an implicit join with the category table (line 97);
    • lines 105–111: a calculation across two relations—the total amount of each order—entirely performed by SGBD: joins, [sum] and [group by] (lines 103–109);
    • lines 115–120: a grouping. [group by p.categorie.nom] groups products by category name; for each group, the number of products ([count]) and the average price ([avg], of type [Double]) are calculated by SGBD (lines 113–117). The category [plongée], which has no products, does not appear: the join with the category table is an inner join ([join]).

    11.8.3. The N+1 Query Problem

    The lazy loading in the example illustrates a problem that plagues any user of a ORM, known as the “N+1 queries” problem: one query to retrieve the N orders, then one query per order to retrieve its customer (and another for its line items). With a thousand orders, this results in a thousand and one round trips to the server, when a single one would have sufficed. The problem is all the more insidious because it is invisible in the code: [commande.getClient().getNom()] does not look like a query. The solutions are those shown in the example: [join fetch], an entity graph, or better yet, a projection that retrieves only the necessary data. Hibernate also offers batch loading ([@BatchSize(size = 20)] applied to a collection, or to the referenced entity class—in this case, [Client]), which, for example, retrieves the customers for twenty orders in a single query. The log SQL helps identify the problem: the same query being repeated numerous times.

    11.9. Changes to the database schema

    11.9.1. The Problem

    Until now, tables have been created by Hibernate after being deleted. This is impossible for a live application: its database contains data that must be preserved when the model evolves (a new column, a new table). It must be possible to migrate the database from one schema version to the next, in a safe and reproducible manner, both on the developer’s machine and on the production server. This is referred to as schema migration.

    Hibernate does not support migrations: it can create a schema, validate it, and make limited updates to it. In the Java world, the standard practice is to handle migrations using versioned SQL scripts, applied by a dedicated tool—most often Flyway or Liquibase—and to have Hibernate verify that the resulting schema matches the entities.

    11.9.2. Schema Management by Hibernate

    The [hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto] property (or the [schemaToolingAction] method in the configuration, which the program below uses) specifies what Hibernate should do with the schema when creating the [SessionFactory]:

    Value
    Constant [Action]
    Effect
    [none]
    [NONE]
    none (default value)
    [create-only]
    [CREATE_ONLY]
    table creation
    [create]
    [CREATE]
    Deleting and then creating tables
    [create-drop]
    [CREATE_DROP]
    such as [create], and deletion of tables upon closing [SessionFactory]: for testing
    [drop]
    [DROP]
    Delete tables
    [validate]
    [VALIDATE]
    Check that the tables and columns of the entities exist, with compatible types; throw an exception otherwise
    [update]
    [UPDATE]
    Create any missing tables and columns

    Jakarta Persistence defines a neighboring property, [jakarta.persistence.schema-generation.database.action], with the values [none], [create], [drop-and-create], and [drop]. The same actions are available programmatically, as we did with [SchemaManager] from [SessionFactory] ([create], [drop], [validate], [truncate]).

    The value [update] is tempting: Hibernate compares the entities to the database schema and adds what’s missing. It has limitations that make it unsuitable for a production application:

    • it only adds: it never deletes a column or table that has become unnecessary, does not modify the type or length of an existing column, and cannot rename (renaming a field creates a new empty column, while the old one remains with its data);
    • it cannot transform data (fill a new required column, split a column into two);
    • what it does depends on the state of the database it encounters: it is impossible to know in advance which commands will be executed, or in what order, and no record of this is kept.

    We therefore reserve [create], [create-drop], and [update] for development and testing, and we use [validate] (or [none]) in production, with the schema managed by scripts.

    11.9.3. Versioned SQL scripts

    The principle behind script-based migrations is simple:

    • each schema change is described by a script named SQL, numbered sequentially: [V1__creation_clients.sql], [V2__ajout_telephone.sql]... Once a script has been applied to a database, it is never modified again: any correction is the subject of a new script;
    • the database contains a history table that lists the versions that have been applied to it;
    • When the application starts (or during deployment), a tool compares the available scripts with the history and applies, in order, those that have not yet been applied.

    The scripts are part of the application’s source code: they are stored and managed along with the rest of the code (in a Git repository, for example). To understand how this works, the [clients] module implements a small versioned script executor, modeled after Flyway; we will then introduce Flyway itself.

    // a customer
@Entity
@Table(name = "clients")
public class Client {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
    private String nom;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 100)
    private String email;

    @Column(length = 20)
    private String telephone;

    protected Client() {
    }

    public Client(String nom, String email, String telephone) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.email = email;
        this.telephone = telephone;
    }

    @Override
    public String toString() {
        String tel = telephone == null ? "pas de téléphone" : telephone;
        return "[%d, %s, %s, %s]".formatted(id, nom, email, tel);
    }
}

    package clients;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URISyntaxException;
import java.net.URL;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.sql.Connection;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Comparator;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.TreeSet;
import java.util.regex.Matcher;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

// A small script runner for versioned SQL scripts, modeled after Flyway: the scripts
// [db/migration/V<version>__<description>.sql] are applied only once, in version order,
//, and the table [historique_migrations] in the database records which ones have been applied
public class Migrations {

     // a migration script
    public record Script(int version, String description, Path chemin) {
        @Override
        public String toString() {
            return "V" + version + " (" + description + ")";
        }
    }

     // the name of a script: V1__creation_clients.sql
    private static final Pattern NOM = Pattern.compile("V(\\d+)__(\\w+)\\.sql");

     // the history table
    private static final String CREATION_HISTORIQUE = """
            create table if not exists historique_migrations (
                version integer not null primary key,
                description varchar(100) not null,
                date_application datetime not null default current_timestamp
            ) engine=InnoDB""";

     // the database
    private final String url;
    private final String utilisateur;
    private final String motDePasse;

    public Migrations(String url, String utilisateur, String motDePasse) {
        this.url = url;
        this.utilisateur = utilisateur;
        this.motDePasse = motDePasse;
    }

     // the scripts in the [db/migration] folder in the classpath, in version order
    public List<Script> scripts() throws IOException, URISyntaxException {
        URL dossier = Migrations.class.getResource("/db/migration");
        if (dossier == null) {
            return List.of();
        }
        List<Script> scripts = new ArrayList<>();
        try (Stream<Path> fichiers = Files.list(Path.of(dossier.toURI()))) {
            for (Path fichier : fichiers.toList()) {
                Matcher m = NOM.matcher(fichier.getFileName().toString());
                if (m.matches()) {
                    int version = Integer.parseInt(m.group(1));
                    scripts.add(new Script(version, m.group(2).replace('_', ' '), fichier));
                }
            }
        }
        scripts.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Script::version));
        return scripts;
    }

     // versions already applied to the database (the history table is created if necessary)
    public Set<Integer> versionsAppliquees() throws SQLException {
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(url, utilisateur, motDePasse);
             Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement()) {
            ordre.execute(CREATION_HISTORIQUE);
            Set<Integer> versions = new TreeSet<>();
            try (ResultSet lignes = ordre.executeQuery("select version from historique_migrations")) {
                while (lignes.next()) {
                    versions.add(lignes.getInt(1));
                }
            }
            return versions;
        }
    }

     // the scripts that remain to be applied
    public List<Script> enAttente() throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException {
        Set<Integer> appliquees = versionsAppliquees();
        return scripts().stream().filter(s -> !appliquees.contains(s.version())).toList();
    }

     // Apply pending scripts up to and including version [cible]; mark the scripts as applied
    public List<Script> appliquer(int cible) throws SQLException, IOException, URISyntaxException {
        List<Script> appliques = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Script script : enAttente()) {
            if (script.version() > cible) {
                break;
            }
            appliquer(script);
            appliques.add(script);
        }
        return appliques;
    }

     // Apply a script and add its version to the history, within a transaction
    private void appliquer(Script script) throws SQLException, IOException {
         // the script's commands, separated by semicolons, without comment lines
        String texte = Files.readString(script.chemin()).lines()
                .filter(ligne -> !ligne.strip().startsWith("--"))
                .reduce("", (a, b) -> a + "\n" + b);
        try (Connection connexion = DriverManager.getConnection(url, utilisateur, motDePasse)) {
            connexion.setAutoCommit(false);
            try (Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
                 PreparedStatement historique = connexion.prepareStatement(
                         "insert into historique_migrations(version, description) values (?, ?)")) {
                for (String sql : texte.split(";")) {
                    if (!sql.isBlank()) {
                        ordre.execute(sql);
                    }
                }
                historique.setInt(1, script.version());
                historique.setString(2, script.description());
                historique.executeUpdate();
                connexion.commit();
            } catch (SQLException e) {
                 // Warning: under MySQL, a schema modification command cannot be rolled back
                connexion.rollback();
                throw e;
            }
        }
    }
}
    • Lines 29–34: A script is described by a record: its version, description, and path;
    • line 37: a script’s name follows the Flyway convention: [V], the version number, two underscores, and a description;
    • lines 40–45: the history table: one row per applied version, with its description and the date it was applied;
    • lines 59–76: the list of scripts. [getResource("/db/migration")] adds URL from the folder to the classpath, which is listed along with [Files.list] (Chapter 5). This code assumes that the folder is a real folder (which is the case when the program is run by Maven from the [target/classes] folder); Flyway can also read scripts from a [.jar] archive. The scripts are sorted by version number: alphabetical sorting would place [V10] before [V2];
    • lines 79–91: versions already applied, read from the history table, which is created as needed ([create table if not exists]);
    • lines 94–97: the scripts that remain to be applied;
    • lines 100–110: the application of pending scripts, up to a given version;
    • Lines 113–138: Executing a script: its commands (separated by semicolons, with comment lines ignored), followed by adding its version to the history table within a transaction. One caveat, noted in the comment on line 133: under MySQL, a schema modification command ([CREATE TABLE], [ALTER TABLE]) implicitly commits the current transaction and cannot be rolled back. If an error occurs in the middle of a script, the database may remain in an intermediate state. This is why it’s best to use short scripts, each containing only a single change.

    package clients;

import jakarta.persistence.PersistenceException;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import org.hibernate.tool.schema.Action;

public class Main {

     // the customer database; MySQL creates it if it does not exist
    public static final String URL = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbclients?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
         // Target version: the latest by default, or the one passed as an argument
        int cible = args.length > 0 ? Integer.parseInt(args[0]) : Integer.MAX_VALUE;

         // the status of the migrations
        Migrations migrations = new Migrations(URL, "root", "");
        IO.println("versions appliquées : " + migrations.versionsAppliquees());
        IO.println("migrations en attente : " + migrations.enAttente());

         // application of pending migrations
        for (Migrations.Script script : migrations.appliquer(cible)) {
            IO.println("migration appliquée : " + script);
        }

         // Hibernate verifies that the database schema matches the entities (validates)
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
                .managedClass(Client.class)
                .jdbcUrl(URL)
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .schemaToolingAction(Action.VALIDATE)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
            IO.println("le schéma de la base est conforme aux entités");
             // The new column is usable
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session ->
                    session.persist(new Client("Dupont", "dupont@example.com", "01 23 45 67 89")));
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session
                    .createSelectionQuery("from Client", Client.class)
                    .getResultList()
                    .forEach(IO::println));
        } catch (PersistenceException e) {
             // The validation error is the cause of the exception
            Throwable cause = e.getCause() == null ? e : e.getCause();
            IO.println(cause.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + cause.getMessage());
        }
    }
}
    • line 16: You can specify, as an argument, the version up to which to apply the migrations; by default, all are applied;
    • lines 19–26: the status of the migrations, followed by their application;
    • lines 29–35: [SessionFactory] is created with the action [VALIDATE]: Hibernate verifies that the database schema matches the [Client] entity. If this is not the case, the creation of [SessionFactory] fails with a [PersistenceException], caused by the validation error (lines 44–48);
    • lines 38–43: the new column is used.

    11.9.5. Generate the scripts with Hibernate

    The SQL scripts are written by hand. However, Hibernate can help write them: it can generate—without executing it—the script to create the schema, or, by comparing the entities to an existing database, the script to update it. This is what the [GenerationScript] class does:

    package clients;

import java.io.StringWriter;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;

// Hibernate generates the script SQL, which creates or updates the database schema
public class GenerationScript {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
         // The action: create (default) or update
        String action = args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "create";
        StringWriter script = new StringWriter();
         // a SessionFactory that writes the script without executing it
        try (SessionFactory _ = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("clients")
                .managedClass(Client.class)
                .jdbcUrl(Main.URL)
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_ACTION, action)
                .property(AvailableSettings.JAKARTA_HBM2DDL_SCRIPTS_CREATE_TARGET, script)
                .property(AvailableSettings.HBM2DDL_DELIMITER, ";")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
             // the script, without removing 4 spaces from its lines
            script.toString().strip().lines()
                    .map(ligne -> ligne.startsWith("    ") ? ligne.substring(4) : ligne)
                    .forEach(ligne -> IO.println(ligne.stripTrailing()));
        }
    }
}
    • line 13: the action, passed as an argument: [create] or [update];
    • line 16: [SessionFactory] is created solely to generate the script; the variable that holds it is never used. Java 22 allows it to be called [_] (anonymous variable);
    • Lines 20–23: the script generation properties, already encountered in the [modele] module. This time, Hibernate connects to the database: for the [update] action, it needs to know the database schema.

    The creation script, generated from the current version of the entity, is used to create a brand-new database all at once (for testing, for example):

    primary key (id)
) engine=InnoDB;

    11.9.7. Flyway

    Flyway is the most widely used migration tool in the Java world (Spring Boot runs it automatically when an application starts if it is present in the classpath). It works exactly according to the same principle as our executor, but is more comprehensive: [V<version>__<description>.sql] scripts are searched for by default in the [db/migration] folder of the classpath, the [flyway_schema_history] history table, and the application of pending scripts in version order. In particular, it adds a checksum for each script, which detects changes to a script that has already been applied; “repeatable” scripts ([R__description.sql], reapplied with each change, for views for example); migrations written in Java, a lock that prevents two instances of the application from migrating the database at the same time, and a Maven extension ([mvn flyway:migrate], [mvn flyway:info]).

    To use it in module [clients], simply add the dependencies [org.flywaydb:flyway-core] and [org.flywaydb:flyway-mysql] (in their latest versions), keep both scripts as is—since they already follow its convention—and replace the use of the [Migrations] class with the following line: [Flyway.configure().dataSource(URL, "root", "").load().migrate();]

    Liquibase, the other commonly used tool, describes schema changes in files XML, YAML, or SQL (the “changelogs”), and can generate the SQL specific to each SGBD. In both cases, Hibernate is configured with [validate] or [none], and no longer modifies the schema.

    11.10. Hibernate and Virtual Threads

    A database query is an I/O operation: while the server is processing the request, the waiting thread does nothing. Chapter 9 presented two ways to avoid wasting threads during these waits: asynchronous programming ([CompletableFuture]) and virtual threads (Java 21). Hibernate’s API, like the JDBC it uses, is blocking: [getResultList] does not yield control until the rows have been read. With virtual threads, this is no longer a drawback: a virtual thread blocked on I/O releases the system thread that was executing it, and thousands of them can be created. Therefore, we write ordinary blocking code, executed by virtual threads.

    One rule must be followed: a session is not thread-safe. It must never be shared among multiple threads: each thread (each task) opens its own session with [SessionFactory], which is itself shared. Hibernate does not always detect simultaneous use of the same session; the resulting errors are unpredictable.

    The [asynchrone] module enforces this rule:

    package asynchrone;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import jakarta.persistence.QueryTimeoutException;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);

             // 1 - two queries executed simultaneously by two virtual threads, each with its own session
            IO.println("--- deux requêtes en parallèle");
            try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                Future<List<Article>> petitsPrix = executeur.submit(() -> sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article where prix < 200 order by prix", Article.class)
                        .getResultList()));
                String hql = "select count(*) from Article where stockActuel < stockMinimum";
                Future<Long> enRupture = executeur.submit(() -> sessionFactory.fromSession(s -> s
                        .createSelectionQuery(hql, Long.class)
                        .getSingleResult()));
                 // get() waits for each task to complete
                petitsPrix.get().forEach(IO::println);
                IO.println(enRupture.get() + " article(s) en rupture");
            }

             // 2 - a transaction executed by a virtual thread, followed by processing of its result
            IO.println("--- CompletableFuture");
            try (ExecutorService executeur = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
                CompletableFuture<Void> traitement = CompletableFuture
                        .supplyAsync(() -> sessionFactory.fromTransaction(session -> {
                            Article arc = session
                                    .createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = 'arc'", Article.class)
                                    .getSingleResult();
                            arc.setPrix(BigDecimal.valueOf(550));
                            return arc;
                        }), executeur)
                        .thenAccept(arc -> IO.println("nouveau prix de l'arc : " + arc.getPrix()));
                traitement.join();
            }

             // 3 - a stream: entities are processed as they are read
            IO.println("--- getResultStream");
            sessionFactory.inSession(session -> {
                try (Stream<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article where prix >= 300", Article.class)
                        .getResultStream()) {
                    articles.forEach(article -> IO.println("lu : " + article.getNom()));
                }
            });

             // 4 - a query that takes too long is terminated after the specified timeout (in seconds)
            IO.println("--- délai dépassé");
            try {
                sessionFactory.inSession(session -> session
                        .createNativeQuery("select sleep(5)", Integer.class)
                        .setTimeout(1)
                        .getSingleResult());
            } catch (QueryTimeoutException e) {
                IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
            }
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • line 25: an executor that creates a virtual thread per task (Chapter 9). The [try] instruction with resources waits for all tasks to finish before closing it;
    • Lines 26–32: Two tasks submitted to the executor. Each opens its own session ([fromSession]) and executes a query; both queries run simultaneously, on two connections from the pool. Their order in the log (lines 3–9) may therefore vary from one execution to another;
    • lines 34–35: [get()] waits for each task to complete and returns its result (lines 10–13);
    • lines 41–50: a [CompletableFuture] (Chapter 9) whose first step—a complete transaction—is executed by a virtual thread ([supplyAsync(..., executeur)]), and the second step displays its result. The record returned by the transaction is detached (its session is closed): its fields can be read, but its associations cannot be loaded;
    • Lines 56–60: [getResultStream] returns a stream: entities are processed as they are read, without forming a list (lines 33–35). This is useful for processing a large number of rows. With MySQL, note that by default the driver reads all rows of the result before returning the first one; for truly progressive reading, you must instruct it to use a cursor (parameter [useCursorFetch=true] of URL and batch size set by [setFetchSize]);
    • Lines 66–69: a maximum execution time, in seconds, set by [setTimeout]. The query (a native SQL query, which we’ll discuss later) takes five seconds; after one second, the JDBC driver interrupts it, and Hibernate launches a [QueryTimeoutException] (lines 37–39). This is the equivalent, for a query, of canceling a task ([Future.cancel], Chapter 9), which would have no effect here: interrupting a blocked thread in the JDBC driver does not interrupt the query currently running on the server.

    For applications that require a truly non-blocking API, there is Hibernate Reactive, a variant of Hibernate that relies on reactive drivers (those from Vert.x) rather than JDBC, and whose methods return [CompletionStage] or objects from the Mutiny library. Virtual threads eliminate this complexity in most cases: that is the approach taken in this course.

    11.11. Transactions and Concurrency

    11.11.1. Transactions

    Chapter 10 introduced transactions: a set of operations that either all succeed or all fail. With Hibernate:

    • every write occurs within a transaction, opened by [session.beginTransaction()] and closed by [commit] or [rollback]. The methods [inTransaction] and [fromTransaction] of class [SessionFactory] handle this for us: they commit the transaction if the lambda completes normally, and roll it back if it throws an exception, which is then rethrown;
    • All commands sent during the transaction (immediate commands via [INSERT], explicit synchronizations via [flush], and synchronization via [commit]) are either committed or rolled back together;
    • A SGBD error is reported as a Hibernate exception, derived from [JDBCException], which encapsulates the driver’s [SQLException]: [ConstraintViolationException] for a constraint violation (primary key, uniqueness, foreign key, [NOT NULL]), [SQLGrammarException] for an error in the order SQL, etc.

    The [transactions] module illustrates the two ways to handle a transaction:

    package transactions;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.exception.ConstraintViolationException;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six records
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);

             // 1 - inTransaction: commit if all operations succeed, rollback if an exception occurs
            IO.println("--- deux ajouts dont le second viole l'unicité du nom");
            try {
                sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                    session.persist(new Article("raquette", BigDecimal.valueOf(80), 5, 2));
                    session.persist(new Article("vélo", BigDecimal.valueOf(450), 3, 1));
                });
            } catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
                IO.println("%s : contrainte [%s] violée"
                        .formatted(e.getClass().getSimpleName(), e.getConstraintName()));
            }
            afficher(sessionFactory, "raquette");

             // 2 - A transaction managed by the code: multiple entries, validated or canceled together
            IO.println("--- transaction annulée");
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                try {
                     // sale of two bicycles: the UPDATE is sent via flush
                    Article velo = session
                            .createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = 'vélo'", Article.class)
                            .getSingleResult();
                    velo.setStockActuel(velo.getStockActuel() - 2);
                    session.flush();
                     // Adding an item with a name that already exists: error
                    session.persist(new Article("pompe", BigDecimal.valueOf(12), 5, 1));
                     // Confirmation of the entire set (this cannot be done here)
                    transaction.commit();
                } catch (ConstraintViolationException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getSQLException().getMessage());
                     // All operations in the transaction were canceled
                    transaction.rollback();
                }
            }
             // The sale of the bicycles was canceled
            afficher(sessionFactory, "vélo");
        }
    }

     // Displaying an item read from the database, with a new session
    private static void afficher(SessionFactory sessionFactory, String nom) {
        Article article = sessionFactory.fromSession(session -> session
                .createSelectionQuery("from Article where nom = :nom", Article.class)
                .setParameter("nom", nom)
                .getSingleResultOrNull());
        IO.println("article [%s] dans la base : %s".formatted(nom, article == null ? "absent" : article));
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 21–24: Two items are added to a transaction managed by [inTransaction]; the second item has the same name as an existing item. Both [INSERT] processes are executed immediately (lines 4–15); the second violates the uniqueness constraint on the [nom] column: MySQL rejects it (line 16), [persist] launches a [ConstraintViolationException]; [inTransaction] rolls back the transaction (line 17) and rethrows the exception;
    • lines 25–28: the exception is caught; [getConstraintName] provides the name of the violated constraint (line 18). This demonstrates the value of having named the constraint;
    • line 29: the racket, which had been successfully inserted, is not in the database (line 23): rolling back the transaction deleted it;
    • lines 33–51: a transaction managed by the code. Two bicycles are sold, and the update is sent to SGBD via an explicit [flush] (lines 29–36); then an item with an existing name is added: the insertion fails (line 43);
    • line 45: the validation is never reached;
    • lines 46–50: in the [catch], the transaction is rolled back (line 45 of the results). [getSQLException] returns the original exception from the JDBC driver, and its message is that of MySQL (line 44);
    • line 53: the sale of bicycles, although sent to SGBD by [flush], was canceled: the bicycle inventory is still 10 (line 50);
    • Lines 58–64: A method that re-reads a record with a new session to view the actual state of the database rather than the entities from the current session.

    After an exception, a session should no longer be used: its persistence context may contain entities in a state that is inconsistent with the database. We roll back the transaction, close the session, and start over as needed with a new session. This is what [inTransaction] does, and what our code does when exiting the [try] block, which closes the session.

    The transaction isolation level is that of the JDBC connection: [REPEATABLE_READ], the default value for MySQL, as shown in the first example. You can change this for the entire [SessionFactory] using the [jdbcTransactionIsolation] method in the configuration.

    11.11.2. Optimistic Concurrency

    Two users are reading the same item, which has a stock of 10. The first user sells one item and updates the stock to 9. The second user, who read the stock value before this update, sells three items and updates the stock to 7: the first user’s sale is lost. This is the problem of lost updates.

    One solution would be to lock the row for the entire duration of each user’s operation (“pessimistic” concurrency): this blocks other users, sometimes for a long time. With Hibernate, optimistic concurrency is generally preferred: nothing is locked, but a check is performed at the time of saving to ensure that the row has not been modified since it was read. The standard way to do this is to add a version number to the entity—a field annotated as [@Version]. Hibernate increments this number each time the row is modified, and adds the condition “the version still has the value read” to the [WHERE] clause, along with the commands [UPDATE] and [DELETE]. If the command does not modify any rows, it means another user has already accessed the data: Hibernate executes a [OptimisticLockException].

    // an item whose changes are tracked by a version number
@Entity
@Table(name = "articles")
public class Article {

    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Integer id;

    @Column(nullable = false, length = 30)
    private String nom;

    private int stockActuel;

     // the version number: incremented by Hibernate each time the row is modified
    @Version
    private int version;

    protected Article() {
    }

    public Article(String nom, int stockActuel) {
        this.nom = nom;
        this.stockActuel = stockActuel;
    }

    public int getStockActuel() {
        return stockActuel;
    }

    public void setStockActuel(int stockActuel) {
        this.stockActuel = stockActuel;
    }

    public int getVersion() {
        return version;
    }
}
    • Lines 16–17: the version number, in the format [int] (you can also use [long], or a date in the format [Instant]). The application never modifies this itself.

    package concurrence;

import jakarta.persistence.OptimisticLockException;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;
import org.hibernate.cfg.AvailableSettings;
import org.hibernate.jpa.HibernatePersistenceConfiguration;
import outils.JournalSql;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = new HibernatePersistenceConfiguration("concurrence")
                .managedClass(Article.class)
                .jdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/hbconcurrence?createDatabaseIfNotExist=true")
                .jdbcCredentials("root", "")
                .property(AvailableSettings.FORMAT_SQL, true)
                .createEntityManagerFactory()) {
             // the table [articles] is recreated with a single item, without a log
            JournalSql.sansJournal(() -> {
                sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().drop(false);
                sessionFactory.getSchemaManager().create(false);
                sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> session.persist(new Article("vélo", 10)));
            });

             // Two users, two sessions: each reads the same item
            try (Session session1 = sessionFactory.openSession();
                 Session session2 = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                IO.println("--- les deux utilisateurs lisent le vélo");
                Article velo1 = session1.find(Article.class, 1);
                Article velo2 = session2.find(Article.class, 1);

                 // User 1 sells 1 bicycle
                IO.println("--- l'utilisateur 1 vend 1 vélo");
                Transaction transaction1 = session1.beginTransaction();
                velo1.setStockActuel(velo1.getStockActuel() - 1);
                transaction1.commit();
                IO.println("stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 1 : %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(velo1.getStockActuel(), velo1.getVersion()));

                 // User 2 sells 3 bicycles based on outdated data (stock = 10, version 0)
                IO.println("--- l'utilisateur 2 vend 3 vélos");
                Transaction transaction2 = session2.beginTransaction();
                velo2.setStockActuel(velo2.getStockActuel() - 3);
                try {
                    session2.flush();
                    transaction2.commit();
                } catch (OptimisticLockException e) {
                    IO.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + " : " + e.getMessage());
                    transaction2.rollback();
                }
            }

             // Solution: User 2 reloads the article in a new session and starts over
            IO.println("--- l'utilisateur 2 relit le vélo et recommence");
            sessionFactory.inTransaction(session -> {
                Article velo = session.find(Article.class, 1);
                IO.println("stock relu : %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(velo.getStockActuel(), velo.getVersion()));
                velo.setStockActuel(velo.getStockActuel() - 3);
                session.flush();
                IO.println("stock enregistré par l'utilisateur 2 : %d (version %d)"
                        .formatted(velo.getStockActuel(), velo.getVersion()));
            });
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • lines 21–25: The table is recreated with a single item, the bicycle, version 0;
    • lines 31–32: Each user reads the bicycle in their own session. The [version] column is read along with the others (lines 3–10);
    • Lines 36–38: The order [UPDATE] from the first user (lines 13–20) writes the new version (1) and contains the condition [version=?] with the read version (0). The row is modified; the entity’s [version] field is set to 1 (line 22);
    • lines 44–48: the second user’s command contains the same condition, with the version they read, 0, whereas the version of the row in the database is now 1. No rows are modified, and Hibernate throws a [OptimisticLockException] (line 33). We explicitly synchronize the session ([flush]) before the [commit] to obtain this exception as-is; if it were thrown during the [commit], it would be encapsulated within a [RollbackException];
    • Lines 57–65: The resolution depends on the application: abort, notify the user, or, as here, re-read the item using a new session (the session that received the exception must no longer be used), and repeat the operation. The restocked inventory is 9 in version 1 (line 41), and the sale of the three bicycles results in an inventory of 6 in version 2 (line 50).

    Two variations:

    • Without a version column, Hibernate can check the old values of the columns themselves: with the annotations [@OptimisticLocking(type = OptimisticLockType.DIRTY)] and [@DynamicUpdate] on the entity, the [WHERE] clause of the [UPDATE] contains the read value of each modified column ([where id=? and stockActuel=?]). This is useful for an existing database that cannot be modified;
    • pessimistic concurrency remains possible when conflicts are frequent: [session.find(Article.class, 1, LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)] reads the row with a [select ... for update] order, which locks it until the end of the transaction.

    package sqlbrut;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                 // 1 - a hand-written SQL query that returns entities
                IO.println("--- createNativeQuery : des entités");
                BigDecimal prixMin = BigDecimal.valueOf(200);
                List<Article> chers = session
                        .createNativeQuery("""
                                select * from articles
                                where prix > :prixMin order by nom""", Article.class)
                        .setParameter("prixMin", prixMin)
                        .getResultList();
                chers.forEach(IO::println);

                 // 2 - a value passed as a parameter: no SQL injection possible
                IO.println("--- tentative d'injection SQL avec un paramètre");
                String nom = "x' or '1'='1";
                long nb = session
                        .createNativeQuery("select count(*) from articles where nom = :nom", Long.class)
                        .setParameter("nom", nom)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println(nb + " article(s) trouvé(s)");
                 // the same query built by concatenation: never do this
                IO.println("--- la même tentative avec une concaténation");
                String sql = "select count(*) from articles where nom = '" + nom + "'";
                nb = session.createNativeQuery(sql, Long.class).getSingleResult();
                IO.println(nb + " article(s) trouvé(s)");

                 // 3 - results that are not entities
                IO.println("--- createNativeQuery : des valeurs");
                List<String> noms = session
                        .createNativeQuery("""
                                select nom from articles
                                where stockActuel < stockMinimum""", String.class)
                        .getResultList();
                IO.println("en rupture : " + String.join(", ", noms));
                BigDecimal valeur = session
                        .createNativeQuery("select sum(prix * stockActuel) from articles", BigDecimal.class)
                        .getSingleResult();
                IO.println("valeur du stock : %.2f euros".formatted(valeur));

                 // 4 - an update statement
                IO.println("--- createNativeMutationQuery");
                int nbLignes = session.fromTransaction(transaction -> session
                        .createNativeMutationQuery("""
                                update articles set prix = prix * :coefficient
                                where nom = :nom""")
                        .setParameter("coefficient", new BigDecimal("0.9"))
                        .setParameter("nom", "arc")
                        .executeUpdate());
                IO.println(nbLignes + " ligne(s) modifiée(s)");

                 // 5 - the session connection JDBC, for standard JDBC code
                IO.println("--- doWork : la connexion JDBC");
                session.doWork(connexion -> {
                    String requete = "select nom, prix from articles where nom = 'arc'";
                    try (Statement ordre = connexion.createStatement();
                         ResultSet lignes = ordre.executeQuery(requete)) {
                        while (lignes.next()) {
                            IO.println("%s : %.2f euros"
                                    .formatted(lignes.getString("nom"), lignes.getBigDecimal("prix")));
                        }
                    }
                });
            }
        }
    }
}

    Comments:

    • Lines 22–27: [createNativeQuery] executes a query (SQL) that returns rows from an entity's table, and the second parameter ([Article.class]) instructs Hibernate to materialize them as entities managed by the session. The column names in the result must match those in the model: [select *] is appropriate here. The query is passed as-is to SGBD (lines 3–6), except that the parameter named [:prixMin] becomes a parameter JDBC ([?]);
    • lines 32–36: an attempt at a SQL injection. The value of [nom] is passed as a parameter: it is compared as-is to the [nom] column, and no record matches (line 16);
    • lines 40–41: the same query constructed by concatenation. The value of [nom] becomes the code SQL, the condition remains true (line 20), and the query counts the six items (line 21): this is a successful SQL injection. As in Chapter 10, a native query must contain only constant text, with values passed as parameters;
    • lines 46–54: queries that return single values ([String], [BigDecimal]): the second parameter of [createNativeQuery] is then the type of the value. For multiple columns, you can specify a record (its components receive the columns in order) or use [Object[].class];
    • lines 59–65: [createNativeMutationQuery] prepares an update statement, executed by [executeUpdate], which returns the number of rows modified. It runs within a transaction: the session’s [fromTransaction] method opens it, commits it, and returns the result of the lambda;
    • Lines 70–79: [doWork] provides access to the JDBC connection of the session ([java.sql.Connection]), for standard JDBC code (Chapter 10): calling a stored procedure, using a driver feature... The cost of the arc has indeed been reduced by 10% (line 40).

    A native query is not portable from one SGBD to another, and Hibernate cannot verify it before executing it: it is reserved for cases where HQL is not sufficient. HQL also covers a large part of SQL (joins of all kinds, subqueries, windowing functions, [union]...), and allows you to call a function from [union] that it does not recognize.

    11.13. Bulk updates, read-only mode, and batches

    Tracking changes comes at a cost: to increase the price of 100 items, you must read all 100 items, modify them one by one, and the session synchronization will send 100 [UPDATE] commands.     package majenmasse;

import articles.Article;
import articles.BaseArticles;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.hibernate.Session;
import org.hibernate.SessionFactory;
import org.hibernate.Transaction;

public class Main {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        try (SessionFactory sessionFactory = BaseArticles.creerSessionFactory()) {
             // The table [articles] is recreated with its six items
            BaseArticles.initialiser(sessionFactory);
            try (Session session = sessionFactory.openSession()) {
                Transaction transaction = session.beginTransaction();

                 // 1 - update HQL: a single order UPDATE; no entities loaded into memory
                IO.println("--- réapprovisionnement des articles en rupture");
                int nbLignes = session
                        .createMutationQuery("""
                                update Article set stockActuel = stockMinimum * 2
                                where stockActuel < stockMinimum""")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbLignes + " article(s) modifié(s)");

                IO.println("--- hausse de 10 % des prix inférieurs à 150 euros");
                nbLignes = session
                        .createMutationQuery("update Article set prix = prix * 1.1 where prix < 150")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbLignes + " article(s) modifié(s)");

                 // 2 - delete HQL: a single command DELETE
                IO.println("--- suppression des articles de plus de 550 euros");
                nbLignes = session
                        .createMutationQuery("delete from Article where prix > 550")
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println(nbLignes + " article(s) supprimé(s)");
                transaction.commit();

                 // 3 - read-only: read entities are not monitored
                IO.println("--- lecture seule");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article.class)
                        .setReadOnly(true)
                        .getResultList();
                articles.forEach(IO::println);
                 // Modifications to a read-only entity are ignored
                articles.getFirst().setPrix(BigDecimal.ZERO);
                IO.println("session modifiée : " + session.isDirty());
                transaction.commit();

                 // 4 - An `update` command (HQL) does not modify entities already loaded by the session
                IO.println("--- update HQL et entités chargées");
                transaction = session.beginTransaction();
                Article pompe = session.find(Article.class, 2);
                session.createMutationQuery("update Article set prix = 9.5 where id = :id")
                        .setParameter("id", pompe.getId())
                        .executeUpdate();
                IO.println("prix en mémoire : " + pompe.getPrix());
                session.refresh(pompe);
                IO.println("prix après refresh : " + pompe.getPrix());
                transaction.commit();
            }

             // 5 - a stateless session (StatelessSession) and commands sent in batches
            IO.println("--- StatelessSession et lots de 3 ordres");
            sessionFactory.inStatelessTransaction(session -> {
                session.setJdbcBatchSize(3);
                List<Article> articles = session
                        .createSelectionQuery("from Article order by id", Article.class)
                        .getResultList();
                for (Article article : articles) {
                    article.setStockActuel(article.getStockActuel() + 1);
                     // Each change is explicitly requested: entities are not monitored
                    session.update(article);
                }
            });
        }
    }
}
